2deb7a54683db612: KUALA LUMPUR: Johor Darul Ta'zim (JDT) continued their perfect start to the Super League season with a commanding 3-0 victory over Terengganu at the Sultan Mizan Zainal Abidin Stadium in Gong Badak on Sunday.
The Southern Tigers needed 26 minutes to break the deadlock when talismanic striker Bergson da Silva found the back of the net.
Three minutes before the interval, Oscar Arribas doubled JDT's lead with a clinical finish.

In the 64th minute, referee Razlan Joffri Ali pointed to the penalty spot after JDT defender Kevin David Medina brought down Gervane Kastaneer inside the box. However, Mateus Gustavo failed to score for the Turtles.
The Southern Tigers struck again through Shahab Zahedi for their third goal.
The win keeps JDT perched comfortably atop the standings with 18 points from six matches, while Terengganu remain ninth with five points from five games.
At the Hassanal Bolkiah National Stadium in Bandar Seri Begawan, Brunei DPMM FC mounted a spirited second-half comeback to edge 10-man Kuching City 3-2.
The hosts got off to a flying start when Dalberto Luan Belo turned in Farris Izdiham Awang Kechik's delivery in the sixth minute.
Kuching City responded through Australian forward Dylan Wenzel-Halls, who restored parity in the 28th minute before completing his brace five minutes into the second half to put The Cats 2-1 ahead.

However, the tide turned against the visitors in the 62nd minute when playmaker Petrus Shitembi, who had already been cautioned for unsporting conduct in the 53rd minute, picked up his second yellow card and was given his marching orders.

DPMM wasted no time capitalising on their advantage as Azwan Ali Rahman pulled the home side level in the 64th minute, and just three minutes later, Dalberto struck his second of the evening to seal all three points.
4de903fa7b228a1b: VILNIUS: Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company in the Baltic state hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

"It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.
"We shall learn more about who gave the order, how it happened, and who was behind it. It is likely that the instigator has already been identified: it is the Russian side," he added.
Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink's military-grade satellite service, for battlefield communications, strikes on Russia-occupied territory, and its interceptor drones.
It also uses SpaceX's parallel Starlink civilian satellite system.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday that Starlink services in his country were still being restored, after complaining earlier this month about partial restrictions he said were impeding the military's ability to defend against Russian invasion forces.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk insisted any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
There have been several recent attacks on sites hosting Starlink services in Europe.
In September, a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablaze with Warsaw claiming sabotage.
In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way, according to prime minister Roumen Radev, amid an opposition claim that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire.
"Separately, on Sunday, a drone entered Lithuania from Poland before exploding in the country's north without causing injury but damaging a car," Lithuanian authorities said.
"According to initial reports, the object entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland," defence minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.
Warsaw had not noted the drone in question, the PAP news agency quoted defence ministry spokesman Janusz Sejmej as saying.

6ee8088091a3aa53: KUALA LUMPUR: Men's pair Aaron Chia–Soh Wooi Yik have again fallen at the final hurdle.
On Sunday, they lost in the Denmark Open final, which was their seventh defeat in their last eight finals on the World Tour.
The world No. 4 pair were outclassed 21-8, 21-11 by Indonesia's Fajar Alfian–Muhammad Shohibul Fikri at the SJF Bank Arena in Odense.
Despite consistently going deep into tournaments, the former world champions struggled to turn final appearances into titles.
Their only triumph in their last eight World Tour finals came at the Singapore Open in June last year, where they defeated South Korea's Kim Won Ho–Seo Seung Jae in the title decider.
Since then, Aaron–Wooi Yik finished runners-up at the Malaysia Masters, China Open and Arctic Open last year.
Their struggles continued this season with defeats in the Malaysia Open, All England and Taiwan Open finals before Sunday's disappointment in Denmark.
They also fell short at the World Championships in New Delhi in August, losing to China's Liang Wei Keng–Wang Chang in the title decider.

Sunday's defeat was particularly disappointing as Aaron–Wooi Yik had entered the final full of confidence after ousting South Korea's world No.1 Won Ho–Seung Jae 21-14, 21-18 in Saturday's semi-finals, raising hopes of another title in Odense.
However, they failed to replicate that form against Fajar–Fikri, who dominated to deny the Malaysians a second Denmark Open crown.
Aaron–Wooi Yik previously won the tournament in 2023, beating Indonesia's Muhammad Shohibul Fikri–Bagas Maulana for their maiden World Tour title.
Despite the defeat, Aaron–Wooi Yik can take positives from their campaign, having reached the final in their first tournament back together after months of playing with different partners.
Their reunion has shown encouraging signs, particularly with their victory over the world No. 1 Koreans, but their inability to consistently deliver in finals remains a concern.
60a5f4c0ab96ab1c: A WARNING from MSCI that it may exclude Indonesia from its stock market indexes — benchmarks used by global financial investors — risks cutting the nation off from international capital and relegating it to an investment backwater.

MSCI stunned investors by proposing that it remove Indonesia from its global stock indexes altogether, months after floating a less severe downgrade from emerging market to frontier over opaque ownership and securities trading practices.

A cut to standalone status would be unusually harsh and rare: Argentina was dropped in 2021 for imposing capital controls, and Russia in 2022 after Western sanctions cut it off from global finance over its invasion of Ukraine.
Indonesia would find itself in a small group of standalone markets that includes Lebanon and Zimbabwe.
Indonesia has been an MSCI emerging market since 1989, and a downgrade of the proposed magnitude would be a huge reversal for a market that until recently was a foreign investor favourite.
Removing the country from major global benchmarks that steer billions of dollars in foreign investment could hurt far more than just its stock market.
"The proposal... goes well beyond what we had considered our worst-case scenario," said Rully Arya Wisnubroto, head of research at Mirae Asset Sekuritas in Jakarta.

The MSCI announcement wiped about US$65 billion off the value of Indonesian equities, with an 11.6 per cent drop on the Jakarta Composite Index — its biggest one-day fall since the Asian financial crisis in 1998.

The shock spread beyond equities, with the rupiah falling as much as 0.8 per cent and some analysts raising the possibility of a central bank interest rate hike tomorrow, when rates had been expected to stay on hold.

"The purpose (of a rate hike) would be pre-emptive, i.e. in order to prevent the expected equity foreign outflows from widening to the fixed income side as well as being exacerbated by resident capital outflows," Citi wrote in a note to clients.

Banks estimate the move could trigger US$3 billion to US$6 billion in passive outflows, with JPMorgan putting the figure at US$4.8 billion and UBS warning active investors could pull another US$15 billion.
More than US$1.8 trillion in assets are benchmarked to MSCI's emerging market indexes, according to the index provider's website.
Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest economy, is the world's top exporter of thermal coal, palm oil and nickel and a major supplier of copper and coffee.
While the country has benefited from rising prices of some of its commodity exports this year, as a net oil importer, its import bills have also soared.

The fallout from the stock index exclusion could also spread to Indonesia's public finances should state-linked companies find it harder or more expensive to raise money, potentially forcing the government to take spending back onto its own books or scale back investment, Citi analysts added.

"We expect the broader economic impact to be predominantly indirect, with external financing representing the most immediate transmission channel," said Irman Faiz, economist at Bank Danamon Indonesia in Jakarta.

MSCI cited opaque ownership, suspected coordinated trading and inadequate enforcement, saying the problems undermine investors' ability to determine companies' true free float and rely on market prices.

The index provider expects the downgrade to go ahead unless a consultation running until next April finds clear evidence of improved governance and market functioning. A final decision is due by next June.

Indonesian authorities have spent much of the year trying to address MSCI's concerns, tightening disclosure requirements and laying out plans to raise minimum free floats. On Friday, the regulator also announced sanctions linked to alleged manipulation in three stocks.
"It's true that MSCI has a strong reputation, and it's also true that we need to pay attention to what they say," said Dradjad Hari Wibowo, the deputy coordinating minister for economic affairs.
"But there's one thing I want to emphasise — they (MSCI) aren't always right."

fdf9d73e56e1c65a: PETALING JAYA: Social media outrage and trial by public opinion pose a growing threat to judicial independence, says the Chief Justice, Wan Ahmad Farid Wan Salleh, who urged judges to focus on delivering justice rather than on winning public approval.

Speaking at an academic lecture for law students at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin in Kuala Terengganu today, he said the judiciary must distinguish between public confidence, which it must learn, and public approval, which it must never chase.
“Our job as judges is not to be popular. Our job is to be right,” he said in his lecture on whether the judiciary can survive the court of public opinion.

He said lengthy judgments were often reduced to screenshots and circulated online, with people forming strong opinions without reading the court’s reasoning. “I would urge you, whatever the case, to read the judgment itself, including the dissent where there is one, before forming a view.”

Wan Ahmad Farid said courts were frequently praised as independent when their decisions favoured one side, but accused of being compromised when rulings went the other way. “That is not analysis. It is pure, unadulterated partisanship at its ugliest.”

He cited the judiciary’s troubled history, including the 1988 judicial crisis and the 2007 “correct, correct, correct” video controversy, saying public suspicion could sometimes be justified. The judicial institution must acknowledge its shortcomings and rebuild public trust through honest self-correction, he said.
“An institution that cannot speak honestly about its own history cannot ask for trust,” the chief justice said.
He cautioned that anticipated online backlash could influence judicial decisions, compromising independence even without direct interference.
Wan Ahmad Farid called for plain-language summaries of judgments, timely publication, transparent complaints procedures and a credible judicial code of ethics.
He said criticism of judicial decisions was healthy, but personal attacks and attempts to portray judges as enemies could erode respect for the institution.

“The court of public opinion operates on popularity and sometimes unverified data. The court of law operates on legality.” Asked whether the judiciary could survive public scrutiny, he gave an unequivocal answer: “Yes.”

e76d6c7770268438: After boycotting Israeli parliamentary elections his entire life, 55-year-old Said Kabat will head to the polls for the first time on Oct 27. For him, the vote is existential — if a right-wing government is returned to power, he fears for the future of Israel's Arab minority, to which he belongs.

The pharmacist from the Arab village of Majd al-Krum in northern Israel used to boycott elections "all the time". "But now, I will go out and vote," he said, concerned that a low turnout among the Arab population would embolden the far-right elements of the current ruling coalition.

Arab Israelis account for about 21 per cent of the country's population, descendants of Palestinians who remained within Israel's borders after the state's creation in 1948. They have long complained of discrimination compared with Israel's Jewish majority.
The close-fought election is sparking calls for a mobilisation push among Israel's Arab population, after their situation worsened under the outgoing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Driven by far-right ministers Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, settlement construction in the occupied West Bank has soared, and their attention is now turning to predominantly Arab areas inside Israel.

In September, land belonging to Kabat's family in Majd al-Krum was the site of a confrontation between residents and Jewish Israelis who came to establish an outpost — a tactic used by West Bank settlers to take control of land.
"In light of the events, whether in Majd al-Krum or other villages, I urge every young person and everyone with a vote to cast it," Kabat said.
In the last election in November 2022, turnout among Arab and Druze voters was around 53 per cent.
In Majd al-Krum, activists like 31-year-old Dana Salameh were touring the village to explain the importance of voting.

"Everyone, even those boycotting and those unconvinced about voting, has begun to see the danger very close to them if this government remains in power. They don't want Arabs in this state at all... whether here or in Gaza or the West Bank."

The Arab vote is expected to be split among four parties running on two lists. The far-left Joint List brings together three parties, while Raam, or the United Arab List, is more open to negotiating with the right. Raam became the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a 2021-2022 coalition, and it could again play a kingmaker role this year.
A recent poll by Israel's Channel 12 projected that the two lists would garner 13 seats in the next parliament. They currently have 10.
For Salameh, the poll is evidence of a growing conviction among Israel's Arab citizens that they are facing "a battle for existence".
Since the start of 2026, at least 175 Arab citizens have been killed in violent crime incidents, according to the Abraham Initiatives coexistence organisation.
The violence is predominantly driven by criminal gangs, with HIBA ASLAN Arab Israelis accusing the police — under the ministerial responsibility of Ben Gvir — of lax enforcement.
"The state has completely withdrawn from the scene," said criminologist Walid Haddad.
In Majd al-Krum, home to about 17,000 people, campaign billboards for the Joint List have popped up bearing the slogan "The change is in our hands."

Several homes in the village face the threat of demolition, reflecting the reality for Arab localities across the country. Israeli authorities say the houses were built without permits or on state-owned land, but Palestinians say permits are near impossible to obtain.
Further south, in the Negev desert, Israeli bulldozers recently demolished around 80 structures housing about 400 people in the Bedouin village of Al-Dahiya.
For Adnan Abu Wadi, who was left homeless with his four children, the demolitions were nothing more than an election stunt.
"People will turn out to vote in large numbers. We will vote as Arabs to change the government and remove the extremists."
The writer is from AFP

d093c14b8fc7648b: CAIRO: Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.

"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
It followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.

Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on Sept 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.

Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role.

fbd64b5ac1f84214: Malaysia's maritime expanse is double our land mass and spans more than half a million square kilometres. Our seas contribute greatly to national wealth, especially as so much of global maritime trade passes through them.

It is odd then that only 63 per cent of our maritime domain has been surveyed to modern high-density hydrographic standards, as National Hydrographic Centre (NHC) director-general Rear Admiral Dr Najhan Md Said revealed in the New Sunday Times yesterday.
Malaysia has only a single hydrographic survey ship to map the remaining 37 per cent of our sea beds.
Worse, the NHC lacks statutory power, as it relies merely on a 54-year-old administrative memo and survives on cabinet whim.
Hydrographic surveys require coordination with various government bodies and the NHC is prone to bureaucratic delays.

The obvious solution is a dedicated Act of Parliament — as recommended in the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Batu Puteh — to establish the NHC as a permanent statutory authority directly under the Defence Ministry that can streamline decision-making and secure its long-term funding needs.
Commercial shipping passing through Malaysian waters which is so crucial to global trade and our economic well-being relies on detailed seabed mapping to ensure navigational safety.
Shifting seabed sand dunes in the narrow and shallow Strait of Malacca and imprecise depth charts can easily lead to ship groundings that will cause catastrophic bottlenecks to global supply chains.

Moreover, the NHC and its vital work protect our national sovereignty and cultural identity since under international ocean protocols, nations cannot defend sea boundaries or name underwater features with mere statements; they need to produce verified survey data.
The NHC has officially registered 17 major Malaysian undersea features such as the Santubong Seamount and the Rafflesia Hill.
Without our own data, foreign entities could map and name features in our maritime zones and introduce foreign names.

The NHC must be better equipped with more naval survey ships. Since the KD Mutiara retired in 2018, the KD Perantau remains the navy's sole survey ship. It has been estimated that relying on one ship alone to chart the remaining 37 per cent of national waters would take 55 years.

While leasing commercial ships utilising NHC funding has brought coverage up from 50 per cent to 63 per cent, such temporary commercial contracts are poor substitutes for a dedicated naval fleet to safeguard long-term national security.

Malaysia cannot fully defend nor profit from waters it has not mapped. Parliament must pass a National Hydrography Act to afford the NHC full legal power, paired with budget commitments for additional naval survey vessels, the better to secure the nation's maritime frontier.

34133d2f1039c8b7: WUHAN: Maja Chwalinska pulled off an impressive comeback to defeat Britain's Sonay Kartal 2-6, 6-4, 6-2 and claim the first tour-level title of her career at the Wuhan Open on Sunday.
The Polish 16th seed trailed by a set and a break before she turned things around to become just the fourth player to win her maiden tour-level title at a WTA 1000 event.
She joins Naomi Osaka (2018 Indian Wells), Bianca Andreescu (2019 Indian Wells) and Victoria Mboko (2025 Montreal) in that exclusive club.
The 25-year-old Chwalinska started the year ranked 146 in the world and provided one of the biggest surprises of the season when she reached the French Open final as a qualifier in June.
The talented lefty will now rise to a career-high No 11 in the world, making her top-20 debut when the new rankings are released on Monday.

Kartal, who was contesting her second tour event back from a six-month hiatus due to a spinal stress fracture, entered Wuhan ranked 170 in the world but will return to the top 50 after reaching the first WTA 1000 final of her career.
The first set was one-way traffic, with Kartal dictating play with heavy hitting from the baseline and Chwalinska scrambling to defend from all corners of the court.
It took three breaks of serve and 45 minutes to give Kartal a one-set lead and send her closer to the biggest title of her career.

Chwalinska found her legs in the second set and began to put pressure on the Kartal serve by employing the methods that helped her knock out her compatriot Iga Swiatek in the semi-finals: extending the rallies, running down every ball, and mixing things up with her smooth touch.
Despite saving 10 out of 13 break points and holding a 2-0 advantage early in the frame, Kartal surrendered the second set after 71 minutes.
Kartal ran out of steam in the decider as Chwalinska broke twice to secure the trophy on her third championship point after a gruelling two hours and 43 minutes.

90c2ec440b8251f4: SAINT PETERSBURG: The Kremlin on Sunday said Ukrainian large-scale attacks on Russian cities will not change its war aims as Kyiv hit Saint Petersburg with the biggest drone attack on Vladimir Putin's hometown since 2022, setting an oil refinery ablaze.

Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot in night-time strikes that killed one person.

The attack came as Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of violating an "energy ceasefire" announced by US leader Donald Trump 76 times as he warned Russia planned a "blackout" in Ukraine before winter.
Kyiv struck Saint Petersburg as its ties with Washington strained massively in recent days, with Trump waiving sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Moscow on diesel.
Ukraine and its European allies have worried the White House is siding with Moscow, which launched Europe's worst war since WWII in 2022.
Saint Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
"Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses," he said.
Flights were restricted at the city's Pulkovo airport, Beglov said, adding that 12 housing blocks were also damaged.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit in the city and Ozon - Russia's second largest retailer - also reported a hit on its logistics centre.

The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.
Ukraine has attacked Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin's dragging offensive but large-scale hits on Russia's main cities are rare.
"The Kyiv regime is putting up a fight, but that cannot change the course of events," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media.
Russia's offensive against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
US-led peace talks have not led to a breakthrough. In a fifth year of war, few see a way out.
Putin appeared in military uniform this week and repeated that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
'Dreadful routine of war'
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking - it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Sergei, another resident of the city who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he told AFP.
"My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I'd better fill up," he said.
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.
Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.
He said a woman and three children were hospitalised "with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning" in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.
"I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire," 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.
"They're getting on my nerves already," he added, referring to Ukraine.
'Bet on war is paying off'
In Ukraine, Zelensky said Russian strikes hit substations in four Ukrainian regions, leaving "tens of thousands of families without power".
Ukrainian authorities said Russian attacks killed at least three people Sunday, including a 27-year-old woman in Zaporizhzhia and two people in the western Volyn region bordering Poland.
The Saint Petersburg attack came a day after Zelensky called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow as he denounced Trump's move to block new sanctions on Russia.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements," Zelensky said Sunday, adding:
"On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting".
Trump this week blocked a package of new sanctions on Russia which was meant to target Putin, as well as Russia's energy and defence sectors.
He also signed an agreement with Moscow this month to buy diesel, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of elections.
"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance," Zelensky said Sunday.
f88bbaad89e83c0d: ISTANBUL: Iran said Sunday it may not endorse a resolution on Yemen being discussed at a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad unless what Teheran considers "fairness and balance" is reflected in the text, Anadolu Ajansi reported.

Speaking on the sidelines of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers meeting, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said "serious discussions" had taken place on Yemen, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
"Saudi Arabia had its views, and we and other countries also expressed our views," Araghchi said, adding that the proposed resolution had not yet been finalised.
"We hope that fairness and balance will be observed in this resolution and the final statement. Naturally, if this does not happen, the Islamic Republic of Iran cannot join this resolution," he said.

Araghchi said a significant bloc of OIC members holds positions close to Saudi Arabia, adding that Teheran had conducted extensive consultations with other member states and that his speech at the meeting had emphasised a solution to the Yemen issue.

Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The conflict has recently spilled into Saudi Arabia, with Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, including its oil infrastructure, following the group's declaration of a maritime blockade in July.

Turning to relations with the US, Araghchi said Iran's conditions had been presented to Washington as part of what he described as a "7-day plan," and that the US had submitted its views, to which Teheran was still preparing a response.
"From our point of view, the 7-day plan is on the table," he said.

"If there is sincerity on the American side — which there is not — the path is clear. If they fulfill those conditions, the strait will reopen on the sixth day and negotiations will begin on the seventh day," he added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz.
The remarks came during the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, where Iraq assumed the rotating presidency of the council from Turkiye.
The meeting brings together foreign ministers and representatives of the 57-member organisation to discuss regional and international issues, including developments in Yemen and Palestine.

Araghchi also said Iran attaches particular importance to neighbouring Iraq and expressed hope that Baghdad's presidency, along with the appointment of a new OIC secretary-general, would give the organisation "new momentum."
He said Teheran expects the OIC to play a constructive role in resolving disputes among Muslim countries.

693cd9028a064980: PETALING JAYA: Children as young as 12 have been recruited by extremists through online games such as Roblox, even as the Islamic State group (Isis) faces declining influence, says counter-terrorism expert Ayob Khan Mydin Pitchay.

Extremists would befriend children on gaming platforms before inviting them to join private groups where they are taught to carry out attacks, said Ayob, a former deputy inspector-general of police who once headed the anti-terrorism unit at Bukit Aman.

"Police recently arrested children aged 12, 14 and 15. They were first recruited through games such as Roblox before joining other groups. That is where they were taught and trained to carry out terrorist attacks,” Malaysia Gazette quoted him as saying.
Ayob was speaking at a convention on Prophet Muhammad's birthday held in Kuala Lumpur.

He said some of the children were led to believe that killing police officers, soldiers and government officials was permissible in Islam. He cited a 2024 case in which a man aged about 20 or 21 attacked a police station with a parang and seized a firearm.
The attacker believed he was doing the right thing and would die a martyr if killed, Ayob said.
He also said that his experience dealing with terrorism since 1995 showed that extremists often rejected mainstream Islamic teachings and interpreted the Quran and hadith to suit their beliefs.
Ayob urged Muslims to follow established Islamic teachings, which promoted moderation and rejected violence.
Extremist beliefs imported from abroad remained a threat, he said, citing the activities of the Jemaah Islamiah militant group in Malaysia in the past.

Ayob said tougher preventive laws were needed to deal with such threats and ensure those involved could be made to undergo rehabilitation. Education and parental supervision were also equally important to prevent extremist groups from influencing youths.
In January, a 14-year-old Singaporean boy was placed under a restriction order after recreating Islamic State attacks and executions in Roblox and GoreBox, Channel News Asia reported.
The boy, who had been radicalised online, had also hoped to travel overseas to fight for the terrorist group, the report said.
c8d49aa0935c2c61: LONDON: Dejan Kulusevski will be back in Tottenham's matchday squad for the first time in more than 500 days for Monday's home match against Coventry as the struggling club hunt their first Premier League win of the season.

1442224f11c479df: VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo XIV addressed thousands of people in St Peter's Square on Sunday, smiling and saying he would resume work "gradually" in his first major public appearance since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pope had part of his right lung removed in the surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli hospital and he was discharged on Saturday.
"I would like to thank all the people who have been praying for me in these days," the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics told the crowd.
"Having overcome this delicate phase, as you know I will now gradually resume my activities," said the pope, who looked well and spoke normally.
A chorus of "Viva il papa!" (Hooray for the pope!) had reverberated across the square as he appeared at the window of his Apostolic Palace for his traditional Angelus prayer and address.
People in the square welcomed the pope's speedy return.
Christopher Butler, 68, a parish priest from Leeds in northern England called Leo a "great shepherd for the Catholic Church."
"I'm concerned he needs to take time to make a full recovery but he's obviously a very resilient man and keen to return to work, to lead the Church and to be a world leader," Butler said.
Soledad Espinosa, 59, from Ecuador, said she was happy to hear that the pope would be allowed by his doctors to visit Latin America next month.
"We are all hoping for his recovery and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is ok and we're pleased," she said.
Norma Grasso, 76, from Argentina, said: "We are waiting for him."
Following the surgery, there had been doubts about a planned papal voyage scheduled for November 6-17, to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where Leo spent two decades as a missionary.
But his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were "no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead."
'ABSOLUTELY SATISFACTORY'
The pope's discharge on Saturday capped days of uncertainty that rattled the Vatican and the world's Catholics, less than two years into the Chicago-born pope's papacy.
Margaritora said Leo was in "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition," estimating another ten days before he is fully recovered.
Margaritora told Vatican News that Leo's tumour had been discovered by chance, during a routine abdominal X-ray that captured the "little spot" at the base of his right lung.
While calling the lung operation "routine", he saluted the pope's commitment to his recovery, saying he "really put his heart and soul into it, like the most motivated patients."
"His determination to achieve a very quick and very effective recovery from every point of view was really commendable," Margaritora said.
The results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

f45ea87b395ad46c: SHANGHAI: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina fought back to beat rising star Rafael Jodar in the final of the Shanghai Masters on Sunday to claim the biggest title of his career.
The gutsy world number 26 from Spain outlasted his tiring compatriot 1-6, 7-6 (7/5), 6-4.
"I don't know what to say, I don't know what I feel. Just like a huge relief," Davidovich Fokina said.
It is a first title at the prestigious 1000 level for the 27-year-old, who extended his winning streak in China to 10 matches after claiming victory at an ATP 250 tournament in Chengdu.
The 20-year-old Jodar, ranked 13 and rising fast, was ruthless to start with.
He reached over his shoulder to save a point before winning it with an overhead smash as he broke for a swift 2-0 lead.
Davidovich Fokina put pressure on his backhand, but Jodar kept calm as his opponent succumbed to a series of errors.
Jodar broke again for 5-1 before closing out the first set after just 27 minutes with an ace.
Davidovich Fokina dropped serve to hand Jodar a 3-2 lead in the second set, but finally came up with some answers in the next game, falling on his back to save a point at the net and level at 3-3.
Both men battled to hold serve in a run of intense rallies, with the duo needing to restart a point during the ninth game when a ball rolled onto the court.
Davidovich Fokina was shouting in frustration but saved two break points to go up 6-5 when Jodar returned into the net.
But the younger Spaniard would not crumble, sending down a dangerous backhand to force a tie-break.
Davidovich Fokina held his nerve in the tie-break to force a decider.
He was suddenly in control, breaking Jodar's serve in the first game.
Jodar grabbed back a break but the older man led 3-2 when Jodar fired long.
Jodar needed a medical timeout for his right thigh at 4-3 down.
He buckled in pain during a must-win ninth game, keeping the match alive for a bit longer but needing a trainer for his left thigh when trailing 5-4.
Davidovich Fokina sensed victory and claimed the title on his second championship point.
"This is going to be a memory for the rest of my life," the victor said during the trophy ceremony.
He also commended his opponent.
"You are 20-years-old but man, you have a future. And you're gonna be here many times."

6e2d95ed18c5d5d3: IPOH: A total of 156 flood victims from 50 families are seeking shelter at relief centres (PPS) in the Larut, Matang and Selama district as of 8pm today.

A navy helicopter is also on standby to provide aerial support if required.

cae50412b5cbcf57: ROME: As in France, violent clashes have broken out in Italy on the fringes of peaceful demonstrations against the high cost of living, German Press Agency (dpa) reported, citing Italian news agency ANSA on Sunday.

023227dcbcf71c22: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Toxic haze from wildfires burning in Indonesia has spiked a demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say, as they work the clock on equipment providing life-saving clean air.
The months-long haze has blanketed parts of South-east Asia, forcing school closures and fuelling a rise in respiratory complaints. Families are now rushing to buy devices to keep indoor air clean.
At AA Alive, a medical equipment company based just outside of Kuala Lumpur, employees were working at full capacity to deliver oxygen bottles, with officials saying sales were rocketing.
“We have seen a 35 per cent increase in sales because of the haze,” Rafina Firdaus, a member of AA Alive’s sales team, told AFP during a visit.
“When I started in the industry, I was shocked to see so many patients who need oxygen tanks,” she said.
The company supplies patients with both oxygen tanks and oxygen concentrators.
An oxygen tank can run for about three hours of continuous use, while a concentrator can be used for about 24 hours.
Md Noor Bin Bujang, 69, spent more than a month in hospital and received his first oxygen concentrator on Thursday evening.
He told AFP that without the oxygen-providing equipment he would have “a shortness of breath, especially with the haze”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Md Noor Bin Bujang watches television while using an oxygen concentrator at his home in Rawang. — AFP pic
Mubassar Khan, a 26-year-old AA Alive technician, said an oxygen concentrator’s filter is normally replaced after 1,000 hours of usage, but the haze’s pollutants have halved its lifespan.

AA Alive currently delivers around 40 rental units per day, and Firdaus said the company was able to meet the increased demands caused by the haze because they have “already experienced it every year”.
AFP journalists saw close to 60 oxygen concentrators and around 20 oxygen tanks that were due for a service or replacement at the company’s showroom and warehouse.
‘Sharp surge’
Experts warn prolonged exposure to haze pollutants could cause inflammation that is harmful to the body, with one classifying the situation as a “multisystem public health threat”.

Juliana Jalaludin, a professor specialising in environmental health at Universiti Putra Malaysia, told AFP she was worried that future generations could “experience a higher burden of respiratory illnesses if they are repeatedly exposed to haze and air pollution, particularly during childhood”.
“The key is to reduce exposure now to protect children’s health and prevent long-term consequences for future generations,” Juliana said.
Air purifier retailers, meanwhile, said sales have jumped since air quality levels started to dip in August during haze conditions.

“Recently, we have seen a 600 per cent increase in sale volume of air purifier sales... from September 28 to October 12, compared to the same period last year,” regional consumer electronics retailer Courts said in a statement.
“Customers are becoming more conscious of indoor air quality and are actively exploring solutions to maintain a healthier and more comfortable home environment,” a Courts spokesperson told AFP.
Singapore-based retailer Gain City said it has also seen “a significant increase in air-purifier demand”.

“Demand began picking up in recent weeks, with a particularly sharp surge from October 9. Sales have since risen to nine times the level recorded at the start of the haze season in August,” the company said. — AFP
33a39808625dc5d3: IPOH, Oct 18 — For five years, a wheelchair was Salinah Osman’s constant companion, confining the once-active massage therapist to a life far removed from the independence she had enjoyed before suffering a second stroke in 2021.

The 58-year-old, originally from Bukit Mertajam, Penang, still remembers the morning she tried to stand up from a seated position, only for both legs to suddenly give way and her right hand to grow weak.

Unlike her first stroke about two decades earlier, the second robbed her of the strength and mobility she needed to practise her profession, which had brought relief and comfort to hundreds of clients through her home-based spa business.

It also kept her away from the community and volunteer work she loved, leaving her dependent on her husband, Md Rasid Mehat, 66, for daily care while she grappled with other health problems, including heart failure and chronic asthma.

“The ordeal was difficult. I could no longer go out to do charity work, and watching my friends continue with it was heartbreaking. From then on, I had to depend on my husband to take care of me,” she told Bernama.
Despite the setbacks, the mother of two refused to give up, seeking traditional treatments and hospital care while praying for a chance to regain her independence.

Her breakthrough came when she learnt about the rehabilitation benefits available to contributors of the Social Security Organisation (Perkeso) who had suffered strokes, prompting her to submit an application.

In a turn of events she had hardly imagined, contributions she had made while working in a factory more than 20 years ago became the key to accessing the treatment she needed. Although she had long left factory work to become a self-employed massage therapist, her past contributions continued to entitle her to protection under the scheme.
In April, Salinah was offered an intensive rehabilitation programme at the Sultan Nazrin Shah Perkeso Rehabilitation Centre in Meru here, with the cost fully covered by Perkeso.

She spent nearly four months undergoing treatment and staying at the centre, supported by her case manager, medical officers and other staff, while using advanced rehabilitation equipment to help her regain movement and strength.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Salinah progressed from relying on a wheelchair to walking with a stick, before eventually being able to walk unaided after returning home. — Bernama pic
“The desire to get back on my feet kept me going. At first, I had to train for hours every day despite my asthma, and I wondered whether I could do it.

“But one day, I began to move my hand and feel my leg again. That was when I became confident that I could recover here,” said Salinah, who has also been receiving a Perkeso Invalidity Pension since November 2006, which has risen from RM269 to RM573.69 a month.

In the final months of her rehabilitation, she progressed from relying on a wheelchair to taking steps with a walking stick. She also completed a computer networking course to help improve her business when she is ready to resume work.
Salinah was discharged on September 3, and just a week later, while at home, she was able to discard the walking stick and walk without it.

Having gone from being bedridden and fully dependent on a wheelchair to regaining her mobility, she is now working towards rebuilding her massage business and returning to the community service that once formed a major part of her life.

Perkeso chief executive officer Datuk Seri Dr Mohammed Azman Aziz Mohammed said the centre offered comprehensive stroke rehabilitation combining clinical expertise, various therapies and advanced technology, adding that it was open to everyone who required stroke rehabilitation, not just Perkeso contributors.
“For insured persons who meet the eligibility requirements, Perkeso will fully cover rehabilitation costs, subject to an assessment of their condition and suitability for treatment.
“Those who do not qualify for Perkeso benefits may still receive treatment at the centre on a self-funded basis, subject to the same assessment,” he said in a statement to Bernama.

Dr Mohammed Azman said treatment costs varied according to each patient’s condition, needs and rehabilitation goals. The centre offers physiotherapy, occupational therapy, hydrotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy, neuro-robotic rehabilitation, psychological support and vocational rehabilitation, including its Return to Work (RTW) programme.

Its advanced equipment includes the Cyberdyne Hybrid Assistive Limb (HAL), Luna EMG, Vibramoov, MetaMotus Galileo platform and Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), as well as brain neuromodulation technologies such as rTMS and tDCS, and NESA.
He said Perkeso also focused on prevention and long-term protection through its Health Screening Programme, introduced in 2013 to help detect non-communicable disease risks early.

Contributors whose ability to work was impaired by stroke could be considered for benefits under the Invalidity Scheme, including a lifelong Invalidity Pension, Invalidity Grant, Constant Attendance Allowance and rehabilitation aids, subject to medical certification and eligibility requirements. — Bernama
ba3e55186a45f8a8: KOTA BHARU, Oct 18 — The Social Security Organisation’s (Perkeso) Employment Insurance System (EIS) helps workers who have lost their jobs rebuild their livelihoods through financial assistance, career guidance and support in securing new employment.

Perkeso deputy chief executive (Operations) Azirruan Arifin said 117,733 jobseekers had secured employment across various sectors between January and August 14 this year through the organisation’s employment support services.

“These services give contributors faster access to job opportunities that match their experience, skills and labour market needs.

“For contributors who need to upgrade their skills, the EIS also provides training support through active labour market programmes, including reskilling and upskilling to improve their employability,” he told Bernama recently.
Azirruan said one of the main challenges was helping jobseekers secure new employment quickly, particularly when their skills and experience did not meet current industry requirements.
He said Perkeso provided financial and training support to help jobseekers overcome these challenges and improve their chances of securing employment.
For EIS beneficiary Hamdi Ismail, 54, the assistance helped him navigate a career transition after he left his job as a bank clerk to venture into business.

Hamdi said the EIS assistance had supported him during his career transition and helped him plan his next steps.

Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan had earlier announced that Perkeso would enhance EIS benefits, enabling contributors to receive total assistance and protection of up to RM25,000 each, effective October 1. — Bernama
a800b88c6b881979: LONDON, Oct 18 — On a recent weekend, Laura Latham eagerly swung her racquet on a padel court celebrating one year playing one of the world’s fast-growing sports now taking hold in the UK.
“I hadn’t ever picked up a racquet in my entire life ... and I just fell in love,” the 42-year-old civil servant, who lives in Stockport in northwest England, told AFP.
“I know that sounds a bit cliche, but I was just welcomed into this amazing community of fabulous people, all ages, all shapes and sizes ... It’s just great.”
Latham is among a growing number of padel devotees in Britain, where its popularity has exploded after lagging behind European neighbours.

A cross between tennis and squash played by doubles teams on courts enclosed by glass or wire, enthusiasts see it as an accessible and social sport, while critics say it is an expensive fad for trendsetters.
Other complaints range from the noise to private equity firms funding its expansion, especially in the United States.
Tennis legend Rafael Nadal and football icon Cristiano Ronaldo are among players as well as high-profile investors in the fast-paced game, created in Mexico in the late 1960s.
As the sport has grown rapidly in parts of the world, it has attracted finance from a growing array of sources, from real estate firms to specialised institutional investors.
Its recent UK growth has sparked friction in some places, most notably London, where several sites with new or proposed courts have provoked pushback from local communities.

“It’s a kind of hedge fund-backed sport, taking over local spaces and sports,” complained Agnieszka Wood, 52, who helped spearhead an ultimately unsuccessful campaign to stop a beloved east London skating park becoming padel courts.
“But what happens if there’s too many padel courts? What happens if you’re taking the spaces from the communities and you’re not replacing them?”
‘Hotspots’
Padel’s growing popularity is unquestioned, with Wood acknowledging even her own children enjoy playing it.
The Lawn Tennis Association (LTA), the sport’s governing body in Britain, announced in May that national participation had surpassed one million, with nearly 2,000 courts now open nationwide.
That compares with just 400,000 players and 870 courts at the end of 2024.
Globally, active player numbers climbed last year to nearly 20 million, according to the 2026 Global Padel Report, making it one of the world’s fast-growing sports.
Last month it debuted as a medal sport at the Asian Games and harbours hopes of featuring at the Olympics.

Italy, Spain, Portugal and Argentina — so-called “padel heartlands” — lead the way, while Britain has become one of several “demand-led hotspots”, a report by an arm of the consultancy PwC and sport app Playtomic found.
“Padel is tapping into the UK’s deep racquet-sport heritage,” consultant Ray Algar, who compiled the 2026 UK Padel Report, told AFP.
His report estimates more than half of UK padel courts are in cities with around a quarter in rural places.
‘Losing places’
Soul Padel is among the companies behind Britain’s boom.
It has opened 16 pay-to-play courts across four sites in central and northern England and Scotland, with seven more surfaces to open imminently.
Host towns include post-industrial places like northwestern St Helen’s and Warrington — a long way from the caricature image of where padel is played.
“Our view was that the sport had landed well in the UK but ... within affluent areas and had been pitched to that kind of crowd,” explained Soul Padel’s founder and CEO Mark Hewlett.
They offer various targeted programmes, including “Soul Timers” for over-50s, “Soul Singles” for singletons and its most popular, “Soul Sisters”, for women.
Its court rental costs vary by venue and scheme.
In Stockport, Latham said she pays £11 (RM60) for her share of some off-peak games, rising by around £5 at peak times.
But in London, the cost is typically higher and seen as prohibitive by some.
In Bethnal Green, residents are campaigning against council plans to install a temporary court in an area popular with roller‑skaters, skateboarders and basketball players.
Meanwhile, displaced skaters remain upset about August’s closure of nearby Barking skatepark.
“There was huge, huge opposition from the people who went there,” musician and skater Eleanor Dunlop, 29, who co-led the movement against the change, told AFP.
“We’re definitely losing places, like third spaces, where you can be and there’s not immense pressure to spend money.” — AFP
602b6cde2ae5849b: JERUSALEM, Oct 18 — Three years after suffering their deadliest single attack, Israelis will deliver their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an October 27 election that could decide if the country moves definitively into hard-right nationalism.

The trauma of October 7, 2023 remains raw across Israel. Faded stickers bearing the haunting smiles of young people killed by Hamas cover station walls and lampposts, and at bustling restaurants, no one bats an eye as patrons dine with their assault rifles, now liberally allowed.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who polls show is in a tight race, is seeking a new mandate after leading a multi-front regional war in response to October 7, with Israel reducing Gaza to rubble, occupying part of Lebanon and, with US help, bombarding Iran.
The relentless Gaza campaign has brought pariah status to Israel in many once-friendly Western countries, and Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.

Even if the public broadly has supported the war’s aims, the effects at home have been much more divisive, including emboldening Netanyahu’s far-right allies bent on reshaping Israel into a religious-nationalist Jewish state.

“I really think that these elections are about the future of the state in a literal sense,” said Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the Israel Democracy Institute.

Netanyahu’s government has ramped up settlements in the occupied West Bank where settlers armed with the blessing of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir have been attacking Palestinians on their lands with only occasional pushback from authorities.
“The state without a monopoly on the use of force is a failed state,” Rahat said.
Netanyahu, who turns 77 on October 21, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.

The wily political operator returned to power in December 2022 bringing in once-shunned ultra-nationalists and quickly tried to rein in the judiciary, which is examining corruption charges that could land him in jail.
The proposed reforms brought out some of the largest protests in Israel’s history in the months before the Hamas attack.
“Everyone in the country has a strong opinion about Netanyahu. People either hate him or adore him,” said Alon Yakter, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University.
“When you want to see who people vote for, the first question you have to ask is their emotional feelings about Netanyahu.”
Anti-Netanyahu in style, not stance
Seeking to unseat Netanyahu is an informal bloc of parties united mostly around their distaste for him.

Netanyahu’s most formidable rival, according to polls, is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who is in many ways his antithesis — a political novice who wants to unite centrists rather than rally a base, and a phlegmatic speaker with halting English and none of the American-raised Netanyahu’s flair for blistering, headline-grabbing speeches.
Eisenkot as well as other opposition leaders have zeroed in on why Netanyahu failed to prevent October 7.
Netanyahu has been rocked by reports he ignored warnings. He vehemently denies the charges, blaming security chiefs who he said failed to wake him up that morning.
Netanyahu “may have his perfect English, but even with perfect English he got us October 7”, Eisenkot, in Hebrew, told a security conference at Reichman University.
Eisenkot’s son died in the Gaza war — offering an unspoken contrast to Netanyahu’s son Yair, a globe-trotting social media provocateur.

The working-class son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern ancestry, a watershed in a country politically dominated since its founding by an elite of European descent.

Opposition leaders have not criticised Netanyahu’s decision to wage war, likely a losing stance in a country where a recent survey found that only 21 percent of the population identifies as anywhere left of centre.
Eisenkot, as military chief during the 2006 Lebanon war, promoted the Israeli doctrine of using massive force even against civilian infrastructure when in areas used by militants such as Hezbollah.

The opposition has instead heavily focused on social issues including Netanyahu’s tight alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jews, a fast-growing segment of the population due to high birth rates that has promoted religious priorities such as keeping public transit closed on Saturdays.
Netanyahu, while personally secular, has allowed religious students to remain exempt from military service, a source of particular resentment when stretched reservists have served multiple tours.

Opposition figure Naftali Bennett, prime minister in a short-lived 2021-22 government, has vowed to end all exemptions to military service and said that social divisions were putting Israel on a “slow-motion suicide mission”.
Hardline appeal
While the opposition attacks Netanyahu over October 7, for some Israelis, the aftermath of the attack shows the government has brought stability.
While Israelis have died in Iranian and Hezbollah retaliatory attacks, fire has stopped from Gaza, even as Israel keeps striking the territory and Hamas remains.
Israel’s economy has boomed since October 7, with construction sites dotting the major cities and the stock market soaring, led by the technology and defence sectors.

Neriah Yarchi, 19, a barber from Bat Yam near Tel Aviv, came of political age after October 7. He said he would vote for far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who wants the “voluntary” removal of Gaza’s two million Palestinians.
“If Gaza had been ours, they wouldn’t have had a place to infiltrate from and there wouldn’t have been a massacre,” Yarchi said.

Netanyahu has sought to seize on his international notoriety, with his Likud party putting up posters of leaders including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an outspoken critic of Israeli policies, that read, “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t let them win.”

Netanyahu has also vowed loudly never to align with parties representing Arab Israelis, who make up around one-fifth of the population and who some expect to turn out in higher numbers after the intense anti-Arab stances of some of Netanyahu’s ministers.
Arab lawmakers broke precedent to be kingmakers in the 2021-2022 government.

If the new election’s results are as close as expected, it could take weeks or months to form a government. Eisenkot has said he would not ally with Arab parties or Netanyahu, but some critics do not believe he would refuse.
Uriel Reichman, a former lawmaker who founded the university bearing his name, told the conference addressed by Eisenkot that a Netanyahu triumph could permanently entrench Israel’s right-wing turn.
He drew a parallel to countries such as Turkey where an elected populist packs the government with loyalists and transforms once-independent institutions.
“Experience shows that once such a system is put in place, it would be extremely difficult to dismantle it,” he said. — AFP
bd3da3eff3ce1dd6: TOKYO, Oct 18 — Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’s moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first-round trip to the Martian region.

The unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Centre Tuesday at 4:41am (1941 GMT Monday), according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa).

The spacecraft will arrive near Mars one year later, where it will orbit its moon Phobos for up to three years before landing and collecting at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material from the surface.
A rover dubbed IDEFIX — the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog — will first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
“The sampling (from) Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means... this is the first round-trip to the Martian system,” MMX’s project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu told AFP.

Jaxa said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars — something “essential for crewed Mars exploration”.
It will also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it will not land on it, before returning to Earth.
Impact or capture
Jaxa hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born.
One theory for the origin of the Martian moons — the “giant impact” hypothesis — is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.
The “capture” hypothesis, meanwhile, postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’s gravity.

Determining which is right will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, Jaxa said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

“MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles, and organic compounds from the outer Solar System to the inner rocky planet region — processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on IDEFIX.

“If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he told AFP.
Deep in the ‘gravity well’
MMX is a collaboration with France’s National Centre for Space Studies (CNES), the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Nasa, the European Space Agency (ESA), and about 20 universities and tech companies.
The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, Jaxa scientists say.

Japan’s unmanned Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM) — the “Moon Sniper” — tipped over after touching down on Earth’s Moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights.

Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including Jaxa’s unmanned Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4 grams of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometres from Earth in 2020.

One of the differences between Jaxa’s past asteroid probes and the MMX mission is that this time “we have to travel very close to Mars and return”, which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu told reporters.
Phobos orbits about 6,000 kilometres above the Martian surface.
“Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said.
China’s mission
US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’s surface back to Earth.
Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples.
The mission, however, was effectively cancelled by the administration of President Donald Trump following a vote by the US Congress in January.
China, meanwhile, has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 — potentially before the MMX’s return.

Jaxa scientists say sand and rocks from Phobos may offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars. — AFP
0bd6844542ca4bf9: PETALING JAYA: A cohesive Gabungan Rakyat Sabah will give the coalition political leverage with the federal government, GRS chairman Hajiji Noor reminded his coalition partners today.
Hajiji said such leverage risked being undermined by political egos or power struggles for positions, Bernama reported.

“There is no point in praising the unity of others if we are still bickering within the GRS fold itself; for the true strength of Sabah begins with our own unity,” he was quoted as saying while speaking at the GRS convention in Kudat.
He said GRS component parties must place the interests of Sabah and the coalition over personal or individual party interests to strengthen the state’s bargaining power at Putrajaya, he said.
Hajiji, who is also the Sabah chief minister, said no component party is so dominant that it no longer needs partners, and that “no party is so small that its contributions can be dismissed”.

He noted that the decision by certain parties to leave the coalition and go it alone should serve as a lesson to strengthen the foundational principles upon which GRS was established in 2020: Sabah's stability.
Hajiji said merely being a local-based party was not enough to win the confidence of voters if the government failed to solve the people’s daily challenges or provide economic opportunities.

“The people want a stable government, one that does more than just talk well, it must be capable of solving problems. We might win the battle of speeches on stage, yet still fail to win the hearts of the people.”
GRS currently comprises six components, namely, Parti Gagasan Rakyat Sabah; Parti Bersatu Sabah; the Liberal Democratic Party; Parti Harapan Rakyat Sabah; Parti Cinta Sabah and Upko.

Last year, Usno quit GRS citing incompatibility with the state government's policies and style of administration. In 2025, Parti Solidariti Tanah Airku (STAR) and the Sabah Progressive Party left the coalition because they disagreed with the electoral pact with Pakatan Harapan.

4b595aa53ce149c7: KUALA LUMPUR: A depleted national rugby sevens squad mustered a sixth-place finish overall in the men's event at the Sri Lanka leg of the Asian Rugby Sevens Series today.
Nik Safuan Ismade Nik Man's squad suffered losses to Thailand (21-15) and Japan (54-5) before bouncing back with a 31-12 win over Uzbekistan in the group stage to advance to the quarter-finals.
Their cup campaign, however, came to an end after succumbing to a heavy 78-0 defeat against heavyweights Hong Kong in the last eight.
The squad bounced back with a 42-17 win over South Korea in their first classification match before losing 33-5 to hosts Sri Lanka in their fifth-place decider.
Nik knew the squad would have their work cut out for them in Colombo.

The squad finished fifth at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games a fortnight ago, equalling their best-ever finish from Indonesia 2018, but it came at a cost as numerous players suffered heavy knocks and picked up injuries during the tournament.
"From the start we knew we had a problem as a number of our core players were not able to come here," said Nik.
"So we are fielding mostly young players between 18 to 19 here to give them competition exposure at this level.
"We don't feel frustrated to lose against Japan and Thailand. We know where we are at.
"Our target was to beat Uzbekistan and hopefully reach the quarter-finals and we have achieved that."
The national women's squad finished ninth overall in Colombo after beating Sri Lanka (10-5) and Uzbekistan (20-12) in their classification matches.
The team lost all three of their group matches against Hong Kong (55-0), Thailand (39-0) and Singapore (19-0).
e519944b4c1b1f29: KUALA LUMPUR: Women's doubles pair Pearly Tan–M. Thinaah put months of injury setbacks and personal heartbreak behind them to claim their first title since January at the Denmark Open today.
The Malaysians defeated Japan's Hinata Suzuki–Nao Yamakita 21–18, 21–11 in 36 minutes in the final at the SJF Bank Arena in Odense to secure their second title of the season.
The victory earned Pearly–Thinaah US$70,300 and made them the first Malaysian women's doubles pair to win the tournament since Wong Pei Tty–Chin Eei Hui in 2008.
For Pearly, standing atop the podium with Thinaah carried added meaning after everything they had endured together.
"I think we are getting stronger again after the past few months. A lot has happened to both of us, with injuries and good and bad things," said Pearly.
"I'm very happy to go through all this with Thinaah. To stand on the highest podium today means a lot to us. But we don't want to stop here. We want to move forward and keep improving."

Their previous title came at the Indonesia Masters in January, when Japan's Arisa Igarashi–Miyu Takahashi withdrew from the final. That walkover victory ended Malaysia's 15-year wait for the crown since Vivian Hoo–Woon Khe Wei's success in 2011.

Pearly's season was subsequently disrupted by a recurring back injury at the Badminton Asia Championships in April, forcing her to miss the Uber Cup, Thailand Open and Malaysia Masters while undergoing rehabilitation.
Thinaah, meanwhile, lost her grandmother on Aug 21 before her pet rabbit, Roger, died three weeks later.
The pair began turning their fortunes around by bagging bronze at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games last month.
They ended Malaysia's 12-year wait for a women's doubles medal at the Games and were the country's only badminton medallists.
In Odense, they identified their quarter-final comeback against India's Treesa Jolly–Gayatri Gopichand as the turning point of their title-winning campaign.
Pearly–Thinaah trailed a game and 14–9 before fighting back to win 14–21, 21–17, 21–11.
"We got too emotional and carried that into a few points. But we reminded each other not to leave any regrets. We didn't want to lose that way," said Thinaah.
"We picked ourselves up and wanted to fight for each rally and each point, and play more aggressively. I think that was the main turning point."
Pearly said keeping expectations in check also helped them handle the final against Suzuki–Yamakita.
"Every pair is getting stronger, faster and more aggressive. Coming into this tournament, we didn't want to put too much pressure on ourselves," she said.
"We just wanted to enjoy our game, the environment and the conditions here. That's what we did."
Thinaah said they would allow themselves a brief celebration before returning to work.
"We're really happy to win this title. We can celebrate tonight with a good dinner, but the focus starts again because we're travelling to Paris the next day," she said.
Pearly–Thinaah will next head to the French Open, seeking to build on their Denmark success.

e64442e8f54feb17: BERA: A 43-year-old man with disabilities was killed after being thrown from his car when it crashed at Jalan Mengkarak Station today.
The victim, Sin Wee Liang, who had blurred vision in his right eye, died at the scene of the 1pm accident. He was travelling alone.

"Investigations revealed that Sin lost control of the car before it skidded towards a hillside on the right side of the road.

41390e7eee8e7d2d: PETALING JAYA: Pasangan jaguh, Pearly Tan-M Thinaah, merangkul gelaran juara Terbuka Denmark, sekali gus menamatkan kemarau 18 tahun Malaysia dalam acara beregu wanita.
Pasangan nombor 5 dunia itu mengambil masa 36 minit untuk menewaskan pasangan Jepun, Hinata Suzuki-Nao Yamakita 21-18, 21-11 dalam aksi final Jelajah Dunia Super 750 di Arena SJ Bank, Odense.
Pearly-Thinaah menjadi pasangan Malaysia kedua yang menjuarai Terbuka Denmark. Kemenangan ini juga membolehkan mereka merangkul dua gelaran siri jelajah dunia tahun ini.
Malaysia kali terakhir memenangi gelaran beregu wanita menerusi Wong Pei Tty-Chin Eei Hui pada 2008.
Ini merupakan gelaran Jelajah Dunia kedua buat Pearly-Thinaah, selepas menjuarai Terbuka Indonesia pada Januari.

Kejayaan ini merupakan satu kebangkitan buat Pearly-Thinaah, yang sebelum ini bergelut untuk mengembalikan prestasi terbaik, selepas Pearly terpaksa berehat selama dua bulan pada Jun lalu akibat kecederaan belakang.

Kemenangan ini mengukuhkan kedudukan mereka dalam senarai kelayakan ke akhir jelajah dunia pada Disember, yang menghimpunkan lapan pasangan terbaik. Mereka kini berada di kedudukan keenam dan dijangka melonjak satu atau dua anak tangga apabila senarai terkini dikeluarkan pada Selasa.
Selaku juara, Pearly-Thinaah akan membawa pulang trofi dan wang tunai berjumlah USD70,300 (RM 287,000).
5e60119fc359108c: TAIPEI: Taiwan said on Sunday it had driven away 16 Chinese coast guard, research and fishing vessels involved in simultaneous "maritime harassment" operations.

An "unusually large" number of Chinese vessels took part in the coordinated operations around Taiwan's main island and Pratas, a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coast guard said in a statement.
Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex the island.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months, deploying record numbers of coast guard, research and other vessels around the island.

Sunday's operation comes after Taiwan's coast guard used water cannons against a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas, in the northern part of the South China Sea, on Oct 1, which sparked an angry response from China.
Taiwan controls Pratas, also known as Dongsha, but Beijing also claims the island along with most of the strategic waterway.
f2bba67463a0950e: KUALA LUMPUR: The drug trafficking case near a place of worship close to the Sentul district police headquarters, recounted in the @Sembangohhyeahh podcast, dates back to 2016.
Kuala Lumpur police chief Datuk Fadil Marsus said three police reports were lodged in connection with the case on July 12, 2016.
Fadil said police detected a video from the podcast that went viral this morning.
The video featured a journalist recounting an undercover assignment to expose drug trafficking activities in the area, while claiming that no action had been taken.
"Based on further checks, the podcast content was a retelling of a guest's journalism experience that occurred in 2016," he said in a statement today.
He said such publicity was unwarranted as it could create a negative public perception of the police and affect the force's image and credibility.
He added that all parties must exercise greater care and responsibility when sharing or disseminating information to the public.
"The police are committed to continuously preserving integrity and public trust in the policing institution for the safety and well-being of the nation," he said.
e8720b7155236e01: PETALING JAYA: A reporter's recollections of a large-scale drug trafficking operation near the Sentul police station a decade ago have raised the ire of Kuala Lumpur police chief Fadil Marsus who described it as unwarranted publicity that "sparks a negative perception of the police force and impacts its image and credibility".

The reporter's recollections were made in a podcast published on YouTube yesterday evening in which he recalled how he had hidden in a vacant temple in Sentul for three to four days to observe the drug-trafficking operation for himself.

In a 2:30s video snippet published on TikTok, the reporter remarked: “What defies logic is that the den was operating openly as a drug distribution hub right in front of a major police station, without being raided at all”.
Fadil said the incident took place on July 12, 2016, and had led to three police reports being lodged. He urged the public to be more responsible when sharing or circulating information.
“The police remain committed to maintaining integrity and public confidence in the institution,” he said in a statement.
In the full YouTube podcast, Azrul Affandi Sobry recollects his experiences as a teacher and how he entered journalism with Berita Harian, earning six awards before he left.
d3a317b2a2af8b9a: SHANGHAI: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina fought back to beat rising star Rafael Jodar in the final of the Shanghai Masters on Sunday to claim the biggest title of his career.
The gutsy world number 26 from Spain outlasted his tiring compatriot 1-6, 7-6 (7/5), 6-4.
"I don't know what to say, I don't know what I feel. Just like a huge relief," Davidovich Fokina said.
It is a first title at the prestigious 1000 level for the 27-year-old, who extended his winning streak in China to 10 matches after claiming victory at an ATP 250 tournament in Chengdu.
The 20-year-old Jodar, ranked 13 and rising fast, was ruthless to start with.
He reached over his shoulder to save a point before winning it with an overhead smash as he broke for a swift 2-0 lead.
Davidovich Fokina put pressure on his backhand, but Jodar kept calm as his opponent succumbed to a series of errors.
Jodar broke again for 5-1 before closing out the first set after just 27 minutes with an ace.
Davidovich Fokina dropped serve to hand Jodar a 3-2 lead in the second set, but finally came up with some answers in the next game, falling on his back to save a point at the net and level at 3-3.
Both men battled to hold serve in a run of intense rallies, with the duo needing to restart a point during the ninth game when a ball rolled onto the court.
Davidovich Fokina was shouting in frustration but saved two break points to go up 6-5 when Jodar returned into the net.
However, the younger Spaniard would not crumble, sending down a dangerous backhand to force a tie-break.
Davidovich Fokina held his nerve in the tie-break to force a decider.
He was suddenly in control, breaking Jodar's serve in the first game.
Jodar grabbed back a break, but the older man led 3-2 when Jodar fired long.
Jodar needed a medical timeout for his right thigh at 4-3 down.
He buckled in pain during a must-win ninth game, keeping the match alive for a bit longer but needing a trainer for his left thigh when trailing 5-4.
Davidovich Fokina sensed victory and claimed the title on his second championship point.
"This is going to be a memory for the rest of my life," the victor said during the trophy ceremony.
He also commended his opponent.
"You are 20 years old, but man, you have a future. And you're gonna be here many times," he said.
47aeb4577d5d685b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Malaysia’s Pearly Tan and M. Thinaah ended an 18-year wait for a women’s doubles title at the Denmark Open today after sweeping aside Japan’s Hinata Suzuki and Nao Yamakita in straight games.

The triumph also saw Tan-Thinaah follow in the footsteps of Wong and Chin, who defeated Indonesia’s Rani Mundiasti and Jo Novita 23-21, 21-12 to win the women’s doubles title in 2008.
Eighteen years later, the Denmark Open women’s doubles crown is finally back in Malaysian hands.

d3f3e31c5610d2b3: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Most temporary flood relief centres (PPS) in Penang, Pahang, Kedah and Perak were closed today as floods improved, with only two remaining in operation in Perak as of 4pm.

In PENANG, Seberang Perai Tengah district officer Datuk Kamarul Haizal Koderat said the only centre at Sekolah Kebangsaan (SK) Seri Penanti in Bukit Mertajam was closed this afternoon, and all 36 victims from 10 families were allowed to return home.

In PAHANG, two PPS in Raub housing 26 evacuees from 11 families were also closed at 1pm today.
