0bc6c3351b2b4b81: SHANGHAI, Oct 18 — Alejandro Davidovich Fokina fought back to beat rising star Rafael Jodar in the final of the Shanghai Masters today to claim the biggest title of his career.
The gutsy world number 26 from Spain outlasted his tiring compatriot 1-6, 7-6 (7/5), 6-4.
“I don’t know what to say. I don’t know what I feel. Just like a huge relief,” Davidovich Fokina said.
It is a first title at the prestigious 1000 level for the 27-year-old, who extended his winning streak in China to 10 matches after claiming victory at an ATP 250 tournament in Chengdu.
The 20-year-old Jodar, ranked 13 and rising fast, was ruthless to start with.
He reached over his shoulder to save a point before winning it with an overhead smash as he broke for a 2-0 lead.
Davidovich Fokina put pressure on his backhand, but Jodar kept calm as his opponent succumbed to a series of errors.
Jodar broke again to go up 5-1 before closing out the first set after just 27 minutes with an ace.
A fighting Davidovich Fokina refused to go away.
He dropped serve to hand Jodar a 3-2 lead in the second set but finally came up with some answers in the next game, falling on his back to save a point at the net and level at 3-3.
Both men battled to hold serve in a run of intense rallies, with the duo needing to restart a point during the ninth game when a ball rolled onto the court.
Davidovich Fokina was shouting in frustration but saved two break points to go up 6-5 when Jodar returned into the net.
But the younger Spaniard would not crumble, sending down a dangerous backhand to force a tie-break.
The duo were neck and neck but Davidovich Fokina held his nerve in the tie-break to force a decider.
He was suddenly in control, breaking Jodar’s serve in the first game.
His celebration was cut short when Jodar grabbed back a break.
But it went his way again when Jodar fired long to hand the elder Spaniard a 3-2 lead.
Jodar needed a medical timeout for his right thigh as he trailed Davidovich Fokina 4-3.
He buckled in pain as he went for a point during a must-win ninth game, keeping the match alive for a bit longer but needing a trainer for his left thigh at 5-4.
Davidovich Fokina sensed victory and claimed the title on his second championship point. — AFP
21062fe420102790: KUALA TERENGGANU, Oct 18 — Department heads in the public service sector can leverage the Hybrid Workday (HBH) Policy to adapt to haze conditions in their respective states.

Public Service Department (PSD) director-general Tan Sri Dr Wan Ahmad Dahlan Abdul Aziz said that department heads may employ appropriate methods under the HBH framework to ensure that work deliverables or Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for every civil servant are met.
“We have already implemented this hybrid work schedule, and in the context of the current haze, it is essentially a matter of the situation coinciding.

“Therefore, it is up to the department heads to make use of this arrangement. We can certainly utilise the HBH Policy. However, the most important aspect is that KPIs must be established to ensure that output is maintained, even when working in a hybrid manner during these haze conditions,” he said following the ‘Santuni Pesara’ programme held around Kuala Terengganu and Kuala Nerus today.
Also present was the Terengganu Federal Development Department director Datuk Abdul Kahar Abdul Latif.

During the programme, Wan Ahmad Dahlan took the time to visit and present cash contributions as well as basic necessities to three families of retired government servants — Soh Kim Seah, 90; and Rosnani Abdullah, 73; and Mohd Saadum Che Embong, 69.

Meanwhile, he said that the provision of a special financial assistance of RM750 to over one million government retirees, as outlined in Budget 2027, demonstrates the government’s concern for the contributions made by this group.
He noted that the contributions of retirees to national development throughout their years of service are of immense value and should not be forgotten.

“This clearly shows that the government has never neglected retirees who have served the nation. The ‘Santuni Pesara’ programme is also one of the initiatives implemented to honour their contributions,” he added. — Bernama
632ea8a3cf541431: TAIPEI, Oct 18 — Taiwan said today it had driven away 16 Chinese coast guard, research and fishing vessels involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.

An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in the coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas, a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coast guard said in a statement.
The Chinese vessels, including four fishing boats, carried out “simultaneous operations at multiple locations and engaged in hybrid warfare,” the statement said.
The locations were off Taiwan’s eastern, southern and southwestern coastlines, and around Pratas. Some of the Chinese vessels entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and also asserts jurisdiction over the waters around the island, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to seize Taiwan.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months, deploying record numbers of coast guard, research and other vessels around the island.

Today’s operation comes after Taiwan’s coast guard used a water cannon against a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas, in the northern part of the South China Sea, on October 1, which sparked an angry response from China.
Taiwan controls Pratas, also known as Dongsha, but Beijing also claims the island along with most of the strategic waterway.
Taiwan’s coast guard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats”.
“China is attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait and create the false impression of jurisdiction,” the statement said.
“Such actions will only lead to resentment among the people of Taiwan, and the Coast Guard Administration condemns them in the strongest terms.”
China began conducting law enforcement patrols in waters to the east of Taiwan in June, which Taipei branded as “provocative” and “expansionism in disguise”.
Beijing has since dialled up pressure, deploying a record 244 coast guard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show.
That compares with 55 ships detected in June and 30 in May, and 58 in July last year. In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected.
About 60 per cent are coast guard ships, with research vessels and other government boats making up the rest.
The figures do not include Chinese warships, which China’s military deploys around Taiwan on a near-daily basis. — AFP
8e6e1b3a66655ed7: KUDAT, Oct 18 — The RM18.7 billion allocated to Sabah under Budget 2027 is not solely for development projects, but also covers the operating costs of federal ministries and departments in the state, Sabah Finance Minister Datuk Seri Masidi Manjun said.
He said a large portion of the allocation will cover operating expenses, including salaries for about 120,000 federal civil servants working in Sabah.
Masidi said the Education and Health departments are the largest recipients of operating funds, together accounting for more than half of the RM18.7 billion allocation.
“The RM18.7 billion is not entirely for development. We need to understand that the allocation also covers the operating costs of federal ministries and departments operating in Sabah.

“So, it would be inaccurate to assume that the entire RM18.7 billion allocation is intended to address water supply problems and other development needs in the state,” he told reporters on the sidelines of the Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) 2026 Convention here today.
According to him, the budget’s development allocation includes funding for both new projects and the continuation of existing projects currently under way.
He added that Sabah’s development needs continue to grow each year, and existing allocations may not be enough to resolve the state’s long-standing infrastructure problems. — Bernama
2c73297beacfa5b2: ROME, Oct 18 — Pope Leo XIV addressed thousands of people in St Peter’s Square today, smiling and saying he would resume work “gradually” in his first major public appearance since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pope had part of his right lung removed in the surgery on Tuesday at Rome’s Gemelli hospital and he was discharged yesterday.
“I would like to thank all the people who have been praying for me in these days,” the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics told the crowd.
“Having overcome this delicate phase, as you know I will now gradually resume my activities,” said the pope, who looked well and spoke normally.
A chorus of “Viva il papa!” (Hooray for the pope!) had reverberated across the square as he appeared at the window of his Apostolic Palace for his traditional Angelus prayer and address.
People in the square welcomed the pope’s speedy return.
Christopher Butler, 68, a parish priest from Leeds in northern England called Leo a “great shepherd for the Catholic Church”.
“I’m concerned he needs to take time to make a full recovery but he’s obviously a very resilient man and keen to return to work, to lead the Church and to be a world leader,” Butler said.
Soledad Espinosa, 59, from Ecuador, said she was happy to hear that the pope would be allowed by his doctors to visit Latin America next month.
“We are all hoping for his recovery and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is ok and we’re pleased,” she said.
Norma Grasso, 76, from Argentina, said: “We are waiting for him”.
Following the surgery, there had been doubts about a planned papal voyage scheduled for November 6-17, to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where Leo spent two decades as a missionary.
But his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were “no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead”.
‘Absolutely satisfactory’
The pope’s discharge yesterday capped days of uncertainty that rattled the Vatican and the world’s Catholics, less than two years into the Chicago-born pope’s papacy.
Margaritora said Leo was in “absolutely satisfactory clinical condition,” estimating another 10 days before he is fully recovered.
Margaritora told Vatican News that Leo’s tumour had been discovered by chance, during a routine abdominal X-ray that captured the “little spot” at the base of his right lung.
While calling the lung operation “routine”, he saluted the pope’s commitment to his recovery, saying he “really put his heart and soul into it, like the most motivated patients”.
“His determination to achieve a very quick and very effective recovery from every point of view was really commendable,” Margaritora said.
The results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky. — AFP

bfa20c62b8bb1167: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Japan’s yuzu, prized for its distinctive fragrance and citrusy tang, is emerging as a potential addition to Malaysia’s halal market, with producers from Kochi Prefecture eyeing new export opportunities.

Director of the Kochi Representative Office in Singapore, Akihisa Ikeda, said Kochi Prefecture participated in the Malaysia International Halal Showcase (Mihas 2026) under the Japan Pavilion, showcasing products that have obtained halal certification.
“While some yuzu products from Kochi Prefecture are already being exported to Malaysia, there are still many untapped opportunities in other sectors.
“This is our first time participating in Mihas, as we seek to tap into the growing demand for halal food,” he told Bernama on the sidelines of Mihas 2026 recently.

Two companies from Kochi Prefecture participated in the event, namely Kochi Ice Co Ltd, which manufactures desserts using yuzu and other citrus fruits, and Umaji Village Agricultural Cooperative, which represents yuzu farmers.
Ikeda said yuzu-based products, which are already popular in Asean countries, still have room for growth.
“Singapore is the first country in Asia to import yuzu products from Japan, and in Thailand, there are many cafes that serve yuzu-flavoured drinks,” he said.
In Malaysia, halal-certified frozen desserts made with yuzu juice from Kochi Prefecture are already sold in Japanese restaurants, he said.
“Yuzu drink and jam from the Umaji Village Agricultural Cooperative are also available in retail outlets in Malaysia, and all these products are halal-certified.

“While most of these yuzu products from Japan are still relatively new in Malaysia, in Europe, especially in France, it is known as a culinary sensation among chefs as they use yuzu seasoning and condiments to enhance flavours in dishes,” Ikeda said.

The Kochi Prefecture, a major yuzu producer in Japan, has been expanding its export market in Europe and the United States, and is now eyeing a larger market share in Asian countries, including Malaysia and Singapore.
According to Ikeda, the producers are targeting consumers who can understand and appreciate the quality and unique features of Kochi’s yuzu produce.

“The fruits are cultivated in the mountain areas of Kochi villages in an ideal environment that produces yuzu fruit with a strong aroma, which is then processed into yuzu-based beverages and seasonings for exports.

“Therefore, there would be no adjustments to price at the moment in spite of rising costs of packaging and other raw materials, as the emphasis would be on maintaining the quality of yuzu-based products from Kochi,” he added.
Ikeda said the producers are focusing on expanding distribution channels in Malaysia, encouraged by the positive market reaction to Japanese yuzu-based products. — Bernama
ab68d03e47fd3127: SINGAPORE, Oct 18 — Residents in Singapore enjoyed a rare day of clearer skies and fresher air today, after a change in wind directions led to an improvement in air quality here.
In its daily haze situation update this evening, the National Environment Agency (NEA) stated that winds had turned to blow from the south.
“However, some smoke haze from Kalimantan continued drifting towards Singapore. Smoke haze was also observed over Sumatra,” the agency said.
At 6pm, the one-hour PM2.5 was in the normal band in the northern region (36), while remaining in the low-elevated band in eastern (67), central (69), western (66) and southern (69) Singapore.
Meanwhile, the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index was in the unhealthy range across Singapore.
The highest reading of 192 was recorded in the western region, while northern Singapore had the lowest reading of 109.
Turning to its forecast for Monday, NEA said showers are expected over Singapore and the surrounding region.
It added that winds are expected to blow from the south-southeast or south, which could limit the transport of smoke haze from Kalimantan to Singapore.
However, the agency pointed out that some smoke haze from Sumatra may still drift towards Singapore.
Data from the Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) shows that the number of hotspots in Kalimantan rose to 110 on October 17, while the number of hotspots in Sumatra fell to 11.
The agency’s 24-hour PSI forecast for Monday is between 100 and 190 — in the unhealthy range.
Despite the possibility of another day of better air quality on Monday, NEA also cautioned that Singapore could again experience smoke haze from Tuesday night.
This is due to a likely change in wind directions to east-southeasterly, which may then bring smoke haze from fires in Kalimantan towards Singapore overnight.
Members of the public are advised to check the latest PM2.5 readings before participating in outdoor activities. — AsiaOne
4b3211cda24acdc7: ALOR GAJAH, Oct 18 — The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) and the Election Commission (EC) have conducted internet connectivity checks at polling centres to test the Optical Character Recognition-Voter Attendance (OCR-VA) system ahead of the Melaka state election, which will take place next month.

State Science, Technology, Innovation and Digital Communications Committee chairman Datuk Fairul Nizam Roslan said one polling centre, Dewan Penyayang at the Lesung Batu Welfare Complex, was found to be unsuitable for the OCR-VA system due to unsatisfactory internet connectivity.
“As such, the polling centre will be relocated to the Machap Baru State Constituency Development and Coordination Committee (Japerun) Complex,” he said.

He was speaking to reporters after the launch of the Barisan Nasional (BN) election machinery for the Alor Gajah parliamentary constituency at Dewan Kampung Permai in Machap Umboo here today. The event was officiated by Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh.
Fairul Nizam said MCMC had also submitted a full report to the EC on internet connectivity at the polling centres to facilitate arrangements on election day.
“I am confident that the EC is fully prepared to use the system on polling day, with assistance from the MCMC,” he said.

It was earlier reported that the OCR-VA system would be used more extensively in the upcoming Melaka state election to automatically record and mark voters’ attendance by scanning information on their identification documents.
The system is expected to expedite attendance verification and recording, reduce errors in manual marking, and improve the efficiency of polling staff and the voting process on election day.
A pilot project for the system was introduced during the Negeri Sembilan state election in August this year.
The EC has set Nov 14 as polling day for the Melaka state election, with nomination day on Oct 31 and early voting on Nov 10. — Bernama
a8370965b9965830: BANGKOK, Oct 18 — Thai authorities have warned of possible flash floods and landslides across Bangkok and 35 provinces as heavy to very heavy rain threatens large parts of the country until October 25.
The Thai Meteorological Department said the wet weather would initially affect southern and eastern Thailand before spreading to Bangkok, central Thailand and other regions from October 21 to 25.

The warning comes as Thailand’s Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM) placed 35 provinces and the capital on alert, with local authorities instructed to prepare emergency response teams and equipment, according to The Nation.
Persistent rainfall is forecast in the south and east from October 18 to 20, with some areas expected to experience heavy to very heavy downpours.

From October 21, rainfall is expected to intensify across the lower northeast, central region, including Bangkok and surrounding provinces, the east and upper south, accompanied by occasional strong gusts of wind.

The department warned that prolonged rainfall could trigger flash floods, sudden runoff from higher ground and landslides, particularly in low-lying areas and communities near foothills and waterways.
Residents have been urged to monitor weather updates and avoid roads prone to repeated flooding.

According to The Nation, eastern provinces including Chonburi and Rayong could face very heavy rainfall on October 21 and 22, while southern tourist destinations such as Phuket, Phang Nga and Krabi are forecast to experience intense downpours later in the week.
The meteorological department has also warned of hazardous conditions at sea, with waves potentially exceeding three metres during thunderstorms in the Andaman Sea and Gulf of Thailand.
Boats have been advised to navigate cautiously and avoid areas affected by thunderstorms.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a monsoon trough over southern Thailand and the southwest monsoon affecting the lower Andaman Sea.
The trough is expected to shift northwards as a high-pressure system from China extends over northern and northeastern Thailand and the South China Sea.

Thailand has already experienced widespread flooding in recent weeks. According to Reuters, floods had killed 71 people since September 16 and affected 51 provinces as of October 12, with about 908,000 households affected.
The latest warning comes as Thailand transitions from its rainy season towards the cooler months, when shifting weather systems can still bring heavy rainfall.
Authorities have urged residents in affected areas to remain vigilant and follow official weather advisories.
c9d703e40af30c27: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Hadoukens, flying kicks and even the iconic car-smashing bonus stage — Street Fighter is back on the big screen, bringing decades of arcade nostalgia along for the ride.

Released in Malaysian cinemas on October 15, the live-action reboot of Capcom’s long-running fighting game franchise recreates the characters, signature moves and memorable moments that have kept fans hooked for generations.
Directed by Kitao Sakurai, the film stars Andrew Koji as Ryu, Noah Centineo as Ken Masters and Callina Liang as Chun-Li, alongside Jason Momoa, Cody Rhodes and David Dastmalchian.
Set in 1993, the story sees Ryu and Ken reunited when Chun-Li recruits them for the World Warrior Tournament, only for the competition to reveal a dangerous conspiracy.
While reactions to the film’s storytelling have been mixed, its colourful characters, elaborate action sequences and numerous callbacks to the games offer longtime fans plenty to look out for.
From faithfully recreated costumes to iconic special attacks and Easter eggs, the reboot leans heavily into the franchise’s gaming heritage.
Round 1, FIGHT! Easter eggs and arcade callbacks
Beyond the fighting, the reboot packs in references designed to resonate with players who spent countless hours battling friends at the arcade.
Ryu’s familiar cry of “Hadouken!” makes its return during combat, while the classic “Round 1, FIGHT!” announcement recalls the start of a match in the games.
Among the more playful callbacks is a recreation of the car-smashing bonus stage from Street Fighter II, with Ken taking part in the destructive challenge.
The sequence references one of the series’ most memorable diversions, in which players could earn points by destroying a parked vehicle within a time limit.
The film also looks beyond the games for inspiration, drawing on the franchise’s cinematic past.
M. Bison delivers a line that recalls a memorable exchange from the 1994 Street Fighter film, in which the villain dismisses the significance of a day that profoundly affected someone else.
The reboot reworks the moment during his confrontation with Chun-Li, acknowledging the earlier adaptation without simply repeating its dialogue.
These references give longtime fans another layer of entertainment, rewarding those familiar with the games and the franchise’s previous appearances on screen.
From Ryu’s red headband to Blanka’s green skin
One of the film’s biggest nods to the games is its attention to the fighters’ distinctive appearances.
Koji’s Ryu sports his familiar white gi and red headband, while Centineo’s Ken Masters retains his signature blond hair and maroon fighting outfit.
Liang’s Chun-Li also stays close to her video game counterpart with a qipao-inspired costume, although her familiar hair ribbons are absent.
Other fighters receive similarly recognisable makeovers, from Momoa’s green-skinned Blanka to Rhodes’ Guile, whose distinctive flat-top hairstyle remains intact.

Dastmalchian’s M. Bison dons a military-inspired uniform complete with a maroon jacket and sweeping cape, while Roman Reigns’ Akuma appears in a dark martial arts gi that reflects the character’s imposing presence.

For fans who grew up choosing these fighters in arcades or on home consoles, the costumes offer an immediate connection to the games, bringing characters once confined to pixels and animation into the real world.
Hadoukens, Shoryukens and the return of signature moves
Of course, a Street Fighter adaptation would hardly be complete without the special attacks that have become synonymous with the series.
Ryu unleashes his signature Hadouken, the energy projectile that has remained one of the franchise’s most iconic moves.
Ken also gets to show off his fighting skills, including the Shoryuken, the powerful rising uppercut that has long been a staple of his move set.
Chun-Li brings her rapid-fire kicks into battle, while Guile unleashes his trademark Flash Kick.
Japanese professional wrestler Hirooki Goto portrays E. Honda, whose sumo-inspired fighting style includes the classic Sumo Headbutt.
The towering Olivier Richters takes on the role of Zangief, whose wrestling-based attacks include devastating throws and the iconic Spinning Piledriver.
Balrog, meanwhile, relies on a more straightforward boxing approach, using heavy punches and brute strength to overpower his opponents.

Bringing these exaggerated attacks into live action is no small feat, requiring a combination of physical performances, fight choreography and visual effects to preserve the moves’ distinctive styles.
The result is a series of confrontations that draw directly from the games, with fighters using the techniques that helped make them fan favourites.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
David Dastmalchian as M. Bison (right) and Curtis ‘50 Cent’ Jackson as Balrog bring the iconic ‘Street Fighter’ characters to life on the big screen. — Picture courtesy of UIP International
From Metro City to a familiar Japanese bathhouse
The nostalgia does not stop with the characters and their fighting moves.
The film’s settings also draw inspiration from the worlds associated with Street Fighter, recreating some of the visual details that helped define the series.

Set in 1993, the story features Metro City, an urban backdrop connected to Capcom’s wider fighting game universe, alongside gritty alleyways and street brawls that evoke the franchise’s classic arenas.
M. Bison’s lavish hotel provides another setting for the fighters to cross paths, offering a contrast to the rougher environments where many of the confrontations unfold.
Elsewhere, a bathhouse and spa setting recalls the traditional Japanese public bathhouse aesthetic associated with stages in Street Fighter II.

Rather than confining its action to a single tournament arena, the film moves between different environments, giving its battles a variety of backdrops while retaining elements of the games’ visual identity.
A nostalgia trip for a new generation

Adapting a fighting game for cinema has always presented a challenge. Unlike story-driven video games, much of Street Fighter’s appeal comes from its competitive gameplay, larger-than-life characters, signature moves and rivalries rather than a conventional narrative.
The 2026 reboot embraces those qualities, and while nostalgia alone may not be enough to win over every moviegoer, it offers longtime fans plenty of familiar details to look out for.

For newcomers, meanwhile, the film serves as an introduction to the colourful world of Street Fighter — a franchise that has travelled from arcade cabinets to home consoles and now back to the big screen.
8321e2250bbface5: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — British singer songwriter Yusuf Islam, better known as Cat Stevens, paid a visit to former prime minister Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad today, following the recent passing of his wife, Tun Dr Hasmah Mohamad Ali.
In a Facebook post, Yusuf said he read Al-Fatihah with Dr Mahathir, noting that the couple had been married for 70 years.
“He is 101 years old, by God’s grace,” he wrote.
The gesture drew warm responses from admirers, many thanking the musician for consoling Dr Mahathir in his grief.

The couple married in Kuala Lumpur on August 4, 1956, after meeting while studying medicine in Singapore.

de4b058085a3d858: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 18 — Educational institutions under the Ministry of Education (MOE) in Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Melaka, Pahang, and Penang will reopen and resume normal operations tomorrow.
In SELANGOR, the State Education Department (JPN) said that outdoor activities are to be suspended, and students attending school are encouraged to wear face masks.

21e8899f3f3dee8c: The Windows command line is a marvelous thing, beloved by administrators, but not quite so welcome when you're trying to get a parcel out of a locker. For the uninitiated, OOHPod is a service where people retrieve and deposit goods in lockers. Scan your ID (or enter it on a touch screen) and the appropriate locker door springs open and the item (or items) can be retrieved. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your perspective), no pop-up keyboard appeared for our reader to unleash havoc (not that they would dream of such a thing), and there was no handy socket to plug in a peripheral. The touchscreen accepted another finger jab, and the command window went away, replaced by the usual OOHPod interface, allowing packages to be collected as normal. It was the responsible thing to do, and the bank of lockers was left in a state where the next customer would not have to worry about what this odd cmd.exe thing was all about. However, the question remains. Would you have been so responsible? 631c78f18e2760a2: In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them a perfectly designed crystal for the job. Unfortunately, that approach doesn’t work well yet, and the problem comes down to data: Most materials consist of crystals, which are 3D periodic arrangements of atoms whose structures are stored in specialized formats, not the text streams that today’s large language models are trained on. The experimental literature is also heavily biased toward a few popular classes of crystals, making AI outputs skew toward those materials. Now MIT researchers have created a multimodal AI model that tackles these problems. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to create rich linguistic descriptions about the structures from experimental research papers and first-principles computational databases. The unified description outlines not just the chemical composition and structure, but also its properties, processing considerations, and potential applications, helping AI learn more about what makes materials impactful. In a new paper in Nature Communications, the researchers showed their system could identify better material designs than models trained on text streams alone by allowing the model to “see” the atomic arrangements and bonding patterns. For example, when the researchers asked the model to identify materials suited for solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolytes, its top results included materials that had been independently identified as promising candidates. The researchers also showed their model learned geometric representations of material structures in ways text-only models could not. “Structure is really at the heart of the materials science field,” says Ju Li, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor in Power Engineering in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE). “If you understand the structure, you can infer quite a lot about the properties and performance of materials. We wanted to build the connection between a material’s atomic structure and its properties and processing for the model.” Joining Li on a paper about the model are Yang Jeong Park, first author and former MIT postdoc; Mayank Kumaran, a recent University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign computer engineering graduate; Chia-Wei Hsu SM ’26; and Elsa Olivetti, the Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor in Engineering in DMSE. Getting models to see in 3D Materials scientists are always on the hunt for new crystals that will lead to the products of the future. Over the last decade, AI has reshaped that process, proposing and designing new crystalline structures, which have highly ordered atomic structures and make up more than 90 percent of solid materials on Earth. Most of those models treat solid crystalline materials as 3D graphs. The rise of large language models has given researchers another tool for innovation. But existing large language models rely heavily on text from published papers and books, limiting their knowledge of the physical world, since many potential crystal structures are stored in computational databases. Text-based models also lack understanding of visual geometry. To overcome those challenges, the researchers decided to create a vision-language model for crystalline materials. They trained a language model to create textual descriptions of crystal structures using an approach known as contrastive learning, in which models compare similar and dissimilar examples of structures and textual descriptions to achieve a unified understanding. This is similar to aligning the visual and language regions of the brain. Following training, the researchers compared the predictions of two versions of the model: one trained on a dataset containing the AI-generated descriptions and the other trained on a dataset containing text from papers only. They found that the model trained on AI-generated descriptions successfully learned how to align geometric structures with text descriptions while the other did not. “We wanted to create an AI model that works broadly across materials,” Li says. “That’s why we decided to synthesize narratives rather than rely solely on existing papers. We found when we used that narrative dataset, the models are better at predicting the function.” Accelerating materials science The researchers then showed their model could be given a natural language query describing a property and identify crystalline materials with that property, outperforming a baseline. “There are sometimes these step changes within materials science around algorithmic integration toward useful tools, which the community uses to further advance the field,” Olivetti says. “This approach helps us see more deeply into three-dimensional structures and link structures to property and processing. I hope this can be one of those step changes.” Li compares the model to AlphaFold, an AI model that links protein structures with function that has helped advance biological research and drug development. The researchers believe their new approach can work with many crystalline materials, and they hope other material scientists will use it to accelerate their work. “Being able to see a three-dimensional crystal and how its atoms are connected is super foundational,” Li says. “I think this will be useful to anyone who practices materials science.” The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Defense Threat Reduction Agency through the University Research Alliance; the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; and the National Research Foundation of Korea.

4a57d3c28cf22595: I’m not shocked by the revelation that some children are refusing to sit next to their Christian or Muslim classmates. I knew it was coming.
On Oct 15, Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin raised concerns in the Dewan Rakyat about religious intolerance among primary school children.
He said a teacher told him that some children said: “I don’t want to sit with them because they eat pork,” or “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross”.

This is far more than a classroom management problem. It is a symptom of a society that is quietly fracturing along ethnic and religious lines — and in Malaysia’s multiethnic reality, that fracture is a national security threat.

In a country where the delicate balance between the Malay-Muslim majority and the Chinese, Indian, and indigenous minorities has historically been the cornerstone of stability, the early crystallisation of “us versus them” at the primary-school level is terribly dangerous, to say the least.

When children are socialised to view difference as a threat rather than a shared reality, the foundation of our society — the mutual accommodation that has kept us together for decades — begins to crumble before critical thinking even develops.
As Mongin warned, if this trend is not addressed at the youngest age, it will inevitably spread, feeding the very 3R controversies that have destabilised Malaysian politics in recent years.
This should not be treated as an isolated case for it reflects deeper structural patterns that threaten Malaysia’s unity.

It is dangerous because it erodes the trust and understanding that underpin social relations, business partnerships and even political alliances. Worse, it creates a radicalisation pipeline: isolated children become vulnerable to extremist online narratives.
I said I knew it was coming. The rise of ethno-religious nationalism, especially since the early 2000s, has amplified our differences.

When an increasing number of politicians unashamedly fire up religion- or race-related issues to win votes or to be seen as champions of their race or religion — and then get away with it or are cheered on by their supporters — what do you expect to happen?
Political rhetoric often frames racial and religious purity as mobilisation tools, and children absorb the tone of such public discourse.
Another reason is that the different communities have moved into their own silos, interacting at work, in school and elsewhere only when and where necessary.

And unlike in the past, the norm today is for children to play or share activities with those of their own race. When school is the only mixed space, and that space is already poisoned by home prejudices or online content, the classroom turns into a battleground instead of a bridge.

Digital poisoning makes the problem worse. Some social media platforms prioritise outrage, with algorithms amplifying hate speech and fake news. Children encounter dehumanising content that normalises rejection of the “other.”
When a pupil says, “I don’t want to sit with them because they wear a cross,” they may have internalised a viral meme or attack on that symbol.
I can go on, but all of us know there are many unspeakable elephants in the room that authorities need to address.
Existing “unity” programmes are well-intentioned but episodic and top-down. They rely on short camps or lectures rather than daily, sustained interaction.

Without structural changes in curriculum and teacher training, they will continue to fail in shifting deep prejudices. Teacher training must include conflict resolution and intercultural communication. Remedies must be structural, not performative as they have been.

Curriculum reform should prioritise critical thinking, media literacy and emotional intelligence over rote “unity” modules. Students need to learn how to deconstruct hate speech and engage in dialogue.
Schools need more group activities to build positive associations.
Digital literacy must become a core subject, not an add-on. Perhaps workshops can be organised for parents on how to guide their children’s online consumption.
Government and civil society must emphasize shared third spaces — mixed sports leagues, arts programmes and community projects — to generate organic positive interactions.
Above all, political leaders must stop exploiting religious and racial divisions for gain. Rhetoric that validates children’s prejudices undermines the very unity they are supposed to defend.

The refusal by six-year-olds to share a desk is small in scale but carries enormous weight. It is a snapshot of Malaysia at a crossroads. If treated as a minor issue, the country risks losing its social cohesion entirely.
If addressed with serious, structural reforms in education, digital literacy and political leadership, genuine unity may be possible.

In a multiethnic society, separation is not merely a social preference — it is a national security threat. Malaysia cannot afford to let its youngest generation grow up believing that difference is a threat rather than a shared reality. The time for action is now.

9fd1af01b713f727: From Moaz Nair

In the noble effort to elevate Bahasa Melayu as the core of national identity, a topic frequently discussed among language enthusiasts is the level of mastery and fluency of the national language among multi-ethnic communities.
Most narratives typically focus on daily communication, the corporate sector, or administrative affairs.

However, from a sociolinguistic perspective, there is a dimension that is rarely explored deeply but carries significant influence over language assimilation: the use of the national language within the religious and cultural expressions of non-Muslim communities.
On one hand, there are high expectations for all citizens to anchor their lives around Bahasa Melayu. On the other, when touching upon the spiritual realm, a more complex dynamic emerges.

Understanding these contrasting approaches is not meant to assign blame, but rather to examine how language can function more inclusively as a bridge for unity without disrupting established socio-religious sensitivities.
Historical framework and the unique situation in the peninsula

The difficulty of expanding the use of Bahasa Melayu in non-Muslim religious affairs in Peninsular Malaysia is rooted in a combination of legal history, demographics, and the evolution of the language's corpus itself.

Under Article 160 of the Federal Constitution, Malay identity is clearly defined by three main elements: professing the religion of Islam, habitually speaking the Malay language, and conforming to Malay custom. This close alignment has caused Bahasa Melayu to evolve with a heavy Islamic imprint over hundreds of years through the absorption of Arabic theological terms into everyday vocabulary.

To preserve harmony and prevent theological confusion, most states in the peninsula enforce the Enactment on the Control and Restriction of the Propagation of Non-Islamic Religions, guided by the principles of Article 11(4) of the Federal Constitution. These laws restrict the use of certain religious terms to ensure the doctrinal integrity of the majority community remains protected.
Aware of these legal and social sensitivities, non-Muslim communities in the Peninsula—comprising largely Chinese and Indian ethnic groups—opt for a cautious approach.

To maintain racial harmony and safeguard their respective theological purity, they feel more comfortable retaining their mother tongues (such as Mandarin or Tamil) or English in their religious affairs. This situation inadvertently creates a linguistic divide in spiritual matters, even though they are fluent in Bahasa Melayu in other daily affairs.
Diverse models in East Malaysia and Indonesia

The reality in the peninsula presents a stark contrast when looking at the socio-political models in Sabah, Sarawak, and Indonesia. In East Malaysia, a unique demographic structure has long positioned Bahasa Melayu as the primary unifying vessel.

For hundreds of indigenous sub-ethnicities such as the Iban, Kadazandusun and Bidayuh, Bahasa Melayu has served as the daily lingua franca, including in church services and their Alkitab (Bible) texts.

The general practice and sharing of religious terms rooted in the same language are accepted with high tolerance as a historical norm, in line with the socio-political guarantees under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63).

Looking at our neighbour, Indonesia underwent a comprehensive language assimilation process because Bahasa Indonesia was established as a neutral and inclusive national asset. There, all recognised religions fully utilise Bahasa Indonesia in rituals and scripture translations.
Major Islamic figures and organisations like Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah play a mature role in guiding society.
They have successfully educated the public by decoupling the language’s function as a national communication tool from the essence of an individual's personal faith.
This approach allows for the harmonious sharing of certain religious vocabularies, anchored by the concept of inter-citizen brotherhood or “ukhuwah wathaniyah”.
Building harmony through mutual understanding
These differing linguistic approaches have a tangible impact on daily social relations. In the peninsula, the separation of language in religious affairs shapes a model of "cautious coexistence".

Multi-ethnic communities deeply respect each other’s boundaries, yet opportunities for deeper cross-cultural dialogue can sometimes be limited by fears of stepping on legal sensitivities. Social interactions remain largely concentrated in secular spaces like economics, education and sports.

Conversely, the dynamics in Sabah, Sarawak and Indonesia demonstrate that when a national language is shared in the most deeply personal aspect of life—spirituality—it can erode suspicion and strengthen a sense of togetherness. The national language is no longer seen as the exclusive property of one group, but as a grand canopy sheltering all citizens.
Conclusion
The desire to see Bahasa Melayu fully embraced by all Malaysians is a noble dream that deserves support. However, discourses on elevating the language must look beyond casual conversation.

We must acknowledge the sociolinguistic challenge that arises when the national language is restricted in non-Muslim spiritual realms to safeguard faith, while simultaneously expecting these communities to assimilate the language into every facet of their lives.

To move forward, the best path is to construct a harmonious, localised understanding. Drawing from the spirit of tolerance in East Malaysia, we can begin to view Bahasa Melayu not as a tool of division, but as a bridge that unites.

Without compromising the legal protections that safeguard the faith of Muslims in the peninsula, the cultivation of the national language in cultural and literary spaces across all communities must continue to be nurtured maturely—for the future of a truly integrated Bangsa Malaysia.

c46893703f4038fb: There is something curious about the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) being shortlisted for the Asian Football Confederation’s (AFC) Member Association of the Year (Gold) award.

Malaysian football has spent months grappling with questions about governance, eligibility and accountability. Now its governing body is in the running for one of the region’s top administrative honours.
The winner will be announced at the AFC’s awards ceremony in Bangkok on Nov 19. FAM shares the shortlist with the FA of Hong Kong, China Limited, and the All India Football Federation.
Perhaps FAM has done enough in certain areas to merit consideration. But what exactly does the AFC reward when it names a member association of the year?
A trophy can recognise activity. It should not substitute for scrutiny of the institution behind it.

AFC general secretary Windsor John says associations submit reports on their activities and programmes. A selection panel awards points for areas such as grassroots development, youth competitions and hosting, with three associations shortlisted in each category.
Asked how the assessment treats governance and accountability, and whether strong programme delivery can offset institutional weaknesses, Windsor said:
“The assessment takes into account a wide range of areas of football in an association. You score high in some, medium in some and probably no score in other areas.”

His answer suggests that the panel assesses associations across several areas, with varying scores. But it does not explain how much weight governance carries, or whether strong results in some categories can compensate for serious weaknesses in others.
That is a fair question about an award meant to recognise an association as a whole. It does not mean the AFC ignored governance when assessing FAM.
The criteria and their weightings should make clear how institutional accountability is judged.
For FAM, the timing makes that scrutiny unavoidable.

The naturalisation scandal has damaged confidence in Malaysian football. Fifa’s sanctions over the eligibility case exposed serious failures that the national association could not brush aside with promises to move on.
The affair raised questions not only about player eligibility, but also about the controls and oversight expected of the body responsible for the national game.

September’s extraordinary congress brought another test. The Football Association of Selangor (FAS) had objected to the eligibility of the electoral committee chairman, a concern also raised by Windsor.

FAM’s electoral code, endorsed at its June 4 congress, states that the chairperson and deputy chairperson of the electoral committee must be qualified to practise law. Yet the congress proceeded amid questions over whether the committee met that requirement.
Electoral rules protect the legitimacy of the process and the people it puts in office. An association that revises its rules must follow them, even when compliance creates an inconvenient problem.
FAM cannot demand respect for its authority while treating its own rules as obstacles to negotiate away.
Governance as part of the scorecard
There is also the AFC’s audit of FAM, which many have urged the association to release in full.

Only part of the report had been presented at the extraordinary congress in June and critics argued that the public deserved to know the full findings, warning that withholding them could fuel speculation.
Prepared by AFC deputy secretary-general Vahid Kardany, the report highlighted weaknesses in governance, accountability and organisational management.
It found that FAM’s administrative structure had not received formal executive committee approval.
It also pointed to decision-making concentrated around certain individuals and critical functions heavily dependent on them.
Weak systems for retaining institutional knowledge threatened continuity and could discourage staff from raising concerns.
These are not cosmetic flaws. A sports association needs clear lines of responsibility, systems that survive leadership changes and an environment where staff can report problems without fear.
Otherwise, the institution risks becoming dependent on a handful of people rather than sound processes.
Football development raises another pressing question.

Malaysia’s U-23, U-19 and U-16 teams have struggled to remain competitive in Asean and reach the Asian stage. Their results demand scrutiny of the system meant to prepare young Malaysians for international football.
The National Football Development Programme (NFDP) was designed to produce a technically superior generation by 2025.
Yet questions persist about its outcomes, coaching standards, talent identification and the number of players progressing to senior international football.
Malaysia has repeatedly reworked its structures while regional rivals continue to develop their talent pools. Academies, coaches and thousands of trainees are not proof of success by themselves.
How many players become professionals? How many earn senior international caps? How many fulfil the promise that justified the investment?
FAM has taken on a greater role in NFDP’s technical implementation. It now has an opportunity to show what a more focused system can deliver.
Another revamp, however, is not an achievement in itself. Results must follow.
The Malaysian Football League’s problems add to the wider unease. Salary arrears and Fifa sanctions involving clubs expose persistent weaknesses in the domestic game.

FAM and the MFL are separate bodies, so responsibility for individual cases must be established rather than casually assigned to the national association. Still, activity reports alone cannot capture the health of Malaysian football.
The AFC may have sound reasons for shortlisting FAM. The nomination does not prove the panel got it wrong, nor does it mean FAM has achieved nothing worthy of recognition.

But an award bearing the title Member Association of the Year suggests more than a tally of activities. If the AFC wants the honour to command respect, it should explain how its criteria assess both an association’s output and the way it governs itself.
FAM, too, should welcome scrutiny rather than hide behind the nomination. Recognition will mean little while questions about its elections, audit findings and development record remain unanswered.
A trophy can decorate a cabinet, but it cannot repair a governing system, develop a generation of footballers or restore public confidence.
Before anyone celebrates the award, the more important question is whether the association has done the work to earn the trust that the honour is supposed to represent.

1fb61941d5b43ee1: From Jason Chuah
Malaysia has staked a good deal of its economic future on a few dozen strands of fibre lying on the seabed.

More than 20 international submarine cables land at over 10 stations in this country, and with its digital economy blueprint the government aims to make Malaysia Southeast Asia’s leading destination for cable landings.
They carry almost all of our international data, including the traffic behind Johor’s data-centre boom. Yet the criminal law that protects them was written for the telegraph.

The only provision aimed squarely at cable damage is Section 431A of the Penal Code. It punishes mischief by cutting or injuring “any electric telegraph cable, wire, line, post, instrument or apparatus for signalling”, with up to two years imprisonment or a fine.
The provision has three serious weaknesses.
First, it requires mischief, meaning intention or knowledge that loss or damage is likely.
A ship that drags its anchor across a cable through carelessness might well fall outside it, and so does one that merely claims carelessness.
That is exactly the explanation offered in almost every recent incident, from the Baltic Sea to the Taiwan Strait. Proving mischief will not be easy.
Second, it stops at the territorial sea. The Penal Code applies to offences committed “within Malaysia”, which takes in our 12-nautical-mile territorial waters but no more.
Its extraterritorial provisions reach Malaysian citizens and Malaysian-registered ships, but not a foreign crew aboard a foreign vessel.
Most of a cable’s route lies further out, in the exclusive economic zone and on the continental shelf.
The Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1984 and the Continental Shelf Act 1966 regulate the laying of cables but do not make damaging them an offence.
A foreign ship that cuts a cable 30 miles off our coast commits, so far as Malaysian criminal law is concerned, no offence at all.

Third, the language is out of date. Modern fibre-optic cables probably count as “apparatus for signalling”. The planned subsea power link carrying a gigawatt of Sarawak’s electricity to Singapore almost certainly does not.

International law regrettably does not fill the gap. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which Malaysia ratified in 1996, is better at protecting the freedom to lay cables than the cables themselves.

Article 113 obliges states to criminalise the wilful or culpably negligent breaking of cables, but only by ships flying their own flags and their own nationals. Malaysia’s law, which ignores negligence, arguably does not meet that obligation.
Worse, Article 97 says that when an “incident of navigation” occurs beyond the territorial sea, only the flag state may prosecute the master or crew.

Nor does it give any right to board a ship suspected of damaging a cable. So when a vessel flying a flag of convenience drags its anchor through a cable in our EEZ, UNCLOS refers us to a flag state that has neither the means nor the will to act.

This is not hypothetical. In May, the director-general of the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency acknowledged that tankers carrying Iranian-linked oil choose to transfer cargo about 70km off Johor precisely to “exploit jurisdictional gaps”.
One monitoring group counted 42 such transfers there in about 10 weeks. They operate in the very waters where Malaysia’s criminal law stops.
The United Kingdom faced the same problem and offers a useful model. Its principal offence dates from 1885 but was long ago extended to the continental shelf.
In May 2026 the British government went further, announcing a new criminal framework covering damage that is intentional or reckless, with tougher penalties.
Malaysia should do three things.
First, replace section 431A with a dedicated offence covering intentional, reckless and culpably negligent damage to telecommunications and power cables, with penalties that reflect what is at stake.
Second, extend that offence expressly to the EEZ and continental shelf, applying to any person, whatever their nationality or flag.
Third, draft it with the enforcement problem in mind.
In August 2026 the Helsinki Court of Appeal revived the prosecution of the crew of the Eagle S, a shadow-fleet tanker accused of cutting cables in the Gulf of Finland.

The court held that the offence was committed where its effects were felt, in Finland. It also held that deliberate anchor-dragging is not a mere “incident of navigation” that UNCLOS reserves to the flag state.

The coastal state suffering the cable damage can therefore have criminal jurisdiction. A Malaysian statute that locates the offence where the damage is suffered, and defines it accordingly, would put our courts on the same footing.
Malaysia, which has long taken a robust view of coastal-state rights, is better placed than the great maritime powers to take this step. What it lacks is a law fit for the age of fibre.
Jason Chuah is chairman of the Board of Research at the Maritime Institute of Malaysia and an FMT reader.

44e84b9497a21540: Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world. In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards. And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos, causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working. Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand. “There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register. Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data. “The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!” A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said. Ransomware with physical consequences Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment. As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks. Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm. “The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register. “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.” BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages. “One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said. The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks. “We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said. AI has entered the chat As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead. Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes. “It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack. Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'” Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.” Industrial orgs increasingly under attack OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit. Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register. The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number jumped more than 87 percent in 2024. Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before. Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2. “The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.” This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems." It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months. Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit' The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments. Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations. This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI, worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.” As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology. “We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register. Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security. Compliance vs. security “There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes. This was prior to the French supermarket hacks. Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations. “So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said. About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that. “The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email. He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.” “The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®
a73522a3fefcaa29: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.

Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.

d9ad1ab514e787dd: From P Kamalanathan
Last week, a young student at AIMST University asked me: “Datuk, did Rajinikanth go to university?”
I smiled.
Rajini studied in a Kannada-medium school and worked as a coolie, carpenter and bus conductor in Bangalore.
He joined a film institute at 25, an age when we tell our youth, “You are late.”
Last week, Jailer 2 was breaking box-office records again. At 74, he is still a superstar.
We celebrate his punchlines, but we ignore his lessons on education.
As a former deputy minister of education who oversaw five million students, I see five lessons from Rajini that our new National Education Plan 2026-2035 is trying to teach.
First: Learning agility beats certificates
Rajini had no degree. But he had what the ministry now calls “learning agility”. From stage plays to learning Hindi for Andha Kanoon to learning motion capture for Enthiran, he never stopped.
In Switzerland this year, I saw Swiss CEOs with no MBAs but 10 micro-credentials in AI. That is the Rajini model: lifelong TVET.
Second: Discipline is education
Director SP Muthuraman once said that Rajini was the first to arrive and the last to leave. In 50 years, there has been no “Rajini late” headline.
We chase tuition, but our students fail because they cannot wake up at 6am. Discipline, like that of the Bangalore bus conductor punching tickets at 5am, is the first certificate.
Third: Humility is Karamah Insaniah
The National Education Plan speaks of Karamah Insaniah, or the recognition and uplifting of human dignity. Look at Rajini.
He is a superstar, yet he sits on the floor, touches elders' feet and says, “I am a small child of K Balachander.”
In an age of TikTok arrogance, he teaches adab. My mother always taught me that education without humility is noise.
Fourth: Reinvention in the AI age

Rajini, at 74, is learning AI filmmaking for Jailer 2. If a 74-year-old can act with de-ageing technology, our youth can earn Google AI certification, which the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) offers free in Selangor.
Fifth: Do well, do good

Rajini famously said, “Money comes, goes. Give.” He built schools quietly. This is what I tell my colleagues at the Public Relations Practitioners Society of Malaysia: sustainability is a competitive advantage. Rajini has sustained a 50-year career because people trust his goodness.
That student asked if Rajini passed his exams. I told him: He did not pass with straight As, but he passed the hardest exam: life.
This Deepavali, when we watch Rajini on screen, let us tell our children:
Don’t copy his style; copy his discipline.
Don’t just whistle for the superstar; learn to be a superstar in your own trade, whether as a welder, coder or teacher.
Because, as Rajini said in Padayappa: “En vazhi, thani vazhi”, or “My way is my own way”.
Let our education system allow every Malaysian child to find their own way.
P Kamalanathan is an MIC central working committee member and a former deputy education minister.

768c5b134c4c2d56: The UK Space Agency needs a name for its Active Debris Removal Mission and has decided that the great British public are the people for the job. The agency confirmed the operation earlier this week and selected ClearSpace UK to lead it. The plan is to remove two UK-registered satellites from Low Earth Orbit, with the clean-up due to begin in 2029. The UK government is backing the effort with more than £60 million, and it expects the disposal to be completed by 2032. The spacecraft will grab each satellite, drop it into a lower orbit for disposal by burning up in the Earth's atmosphe, then climb to a higher one to await its next job. Less suicide dive, more cosmic bin round. And because it’s refuellable, the UK government says it "can help make a difference and sweep space for years to come." Launch is planned from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland. But first, the quest needs a name. The Active Debris Removal Mission hardly trips off the tongue, and the UK Space Agency gave inspirational examples of other project names, such as NASA's Mercury program (named after the Roman god) or Tim Peake's Principia mission (inspired by Sir Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica). Oddly, the agency didn't mention the poll to brand a scientific research ship, which was eventually named Sir David Attenborough rather than Boaty McBoatface, the most popular suggestion. The tag must consist of two words – so no "Itsy bitsy teeny weeny orbit debris clear machiney" – and 150 words to explain the name and how it reflects the theme. So no backronyms, for example Broom (British Robotic Orbital Object Manipulator). Starry McBinface? Obviously, swear words are not allowed, nor is anything deemed "potentially offensive" or political. Using anything that might attract copyright or intellectual property lawyers is also out. Letting the public suggest a name feels potentially riskier than the mission itself, though it should generate some engagement. It's a high-risk, high-reward campaign; there are plenty of dead satellites cluttering orbit, and the ability to remove them is becoming increasingly important. Rob Atchison, Managing Director of ClearSpace UK, said, "Our next step is to design, build and test a spacecraft that can get close, safely, to an object never designed to be caught, and take control of it." If you're getting a sense of déjà vu about this expedition, you're probably right. The European Space Agency (ESA) announced ClearSpace-1 in 2019, which the agency called "the first space mission to remove an item of debris from orbit" with a launch set for 2025. At the time, ClearSpace founder and CEO Luc Piguet said: "This is the right time for such a mission." In latest announcement, Piguet called the UKSA's selection "an important milestone." This is far from the first mission to grapple an object in orbit. Most recently, Katalyst Space sent its LINK spacecraft to rescue NASA's Swift observatory. That was intended to capture the Swift spacecraft and raise its altitude, but failures with LINK doomed it. Perhaps things might have gone better if the public had been given an opportunity to name the spacecraft? ®

814a9ce3b76d1166: Apabila sesebuah kerajaan Malaysia memasuki tahun ketiga pemerintahan dan membentangkan belanjawan untuk tahun berikutnya, ada satu soalan yang lazim ditanya, apatah lagi jika belanjawan menawarkan pelbagai inisiatif yang dilihat baik untuk rakyat. Lalu Hamzah mendakwa bantuan atau 'gula-gula' bukan faktor penentu undi.

Kata-kata itu meskipun boleh dilihat sebagai perli dan menyerang kerajaan, mungkin juga disuarakan untuk menenangkan pembangkang, jika mereka sudah cemas. Juga menaikkan semangat untuk melawan. Pendapat saya mudah: Tak kisahlah bajet pilihan raya atau bukan, janji rakyat dapat manfaat.

Lantas saya setuju dengan pandangan kawan lama saya, Kassim Muhamad, bahawa gagasan ekonomi tidak semestinya kedengaran berdegum-degum. Belanjawan yang manusiawi juga gagasan ekonomi kerana ia melibatkan orang biasa.

"Bagi sesetengah orang gagasan ekonomi mestilah kedengaran gah dan besar biar berdegum. Bagi orang biasa seperti saya, nasib orang biasa yang bergelut mencari sesuap nasi, segala bentuk bantuan itu sangat bermakna," kata si kawan lama.

Bagi beliau ini bukan belanjawan pilihan raya. Ia bajet yang punya sifat manusiawi. Ini elemen penting walau apa pun bajet itu digelar.

e3450c0821b6e75b: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim likes to quote renowned thinkers in his speeches. Critics have said he likes to parade his erudition, which they argue is pointless because he fails to follow through with implementation.

In his budget speech the other day, he cited Isaiah Berlin, the Latvia-born and English-naturalised philosopher, famed for inventing the “hedgehog and the fox” metaphor in a celebrated essay on Leo Tolstoy’s meditation on history.

Berlin divided history’s seminal thinkers into hedgehogs and foxes: hedgehogs being those who relate everything to a central vision (Marx, Nietzsche); while foxes (Shakespeare, Montaigne, Sophocles) pursue multiform, even contradictory, insights to their finale.
He held that Tolstoy was a fox, a brilliant discerner of particularities, who towards the end of his life flirted with disaster by trying to be a hedgehog.

The metaphor sheds light on the concerns raised by Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin about schoolchildren refusing to sit next to classmates because they eat prohibited foods or wear religious symbols of other faiths.
Willie did not say from where the aversion stemmed but few would have difficulty in knowing the motivation.

Interestingly, the problem of polarisation among school pupils can be helped by understanding Berlin’s musings. He said that human beings have to be both hedgehogs and foxes; we maim our sensibility if we choose the exclusivity of the one and dissolve into nihilism if, fox-like, we opt for contradictions that lead nowhere.
Willie has highlighted a problem during the tenure of a prime minister who, in his youth, championed a cause that has contributed to the dilemma facing our education system.
Fortunately, the same leader has access to the ideas needed to free those trapped by a form of exclusivity that harms. He is aware of the way out. Would that he opted for it.
Our children should be open to being both hedgehog and fox.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
