ac4fce70c466a220: The US' bankruptcy courts are currently down owing to what officials are calling a “cybersecurity incident.” The Administrative Office of the US Courts said the websites and systems that support the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC), which manages electronic comms related to bankruptcy cases, were pulled offline while the vendor investigates. BAE Systems runs the affected systems and websites on behalf of the Federal Judiciary, and is “working to restore operations,” according to an announcement by the US Courts on Thursday. “As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service," it said. “The incident has also halted the BNC’s production and distribution of bankruptcy notices for bankruptcy courts.” While the public notice was published on Thursday, the issues affecting the BNC systems began a few days earlier, on October 9, according to the Bankruptcy Court of the Eastern District of Texas. Alongside its own announcement, the same court published a general order indicating that for any case filed on or after September 14 with an active motion to stay, that delay would be extended by an additional 30 days. The court said it will continue to accept filings, open cases, and process documents, but said there may be a delay in the entry and service of notices and orders until the issues are resolved. The courts' ability to process electronic and paper bankruptcy notices is affected, and it applies to federal bankruptcy courts across the country. A spokesperson at BAE told The Register: "BAE Systems, Inc. operates the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) on behalf of the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts (AOUSC). We are aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it. We are coordinating closely with AOUSC on the response." The disruption comes at a difficult time for the US public sector, which has struggled with multiple recent cyberattacks. ShinyHunters' attack on the FBI in September is doubtless the most high-profile of these, although the Arizona Judicial Branch confirmed an attack on the state’s court systems at around the same time. Officials said the “criminal hackers or their bots” were responsible for stealing personal data and backup court files. The US Courts also said in August 2025 that it was stepping up its cybersecurity measures in response to increased targeting of its case management system. ®
a280835cafd4ef1b: The UK's competition watchdog wants to designate Microsoft with strategic market status (SMS) in business software, allowing the regulator it to intervene to level the playing field, and says it is considering other areas for investigation. Regulators around the world are watching to see what the UK decides in this case, with bodies such as the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the European Commission mulling similar actions. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications. This follows an investigation the regulator started back in May into Microsoft’s software portfolio including Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint and Teams, plus its security, server and operating systems. The watchdog is also probing whether Microsoft enjoys a position of “substantial and entrenched market power” through the suite of software that could be seen as stifling competition and harming buyer choice. It lays out its proposed decision in a document [PDF] and is inviting comments that must be submitted by November 13. The CMA will make its final decision by February 13, 2027. Bargain spotter The CMA makes it clear the company holds a strong position in each of the five areas it investigated (personal computer operating systems, productivity software suites, security software, server operating systems and relational database management systems), and that customers face barriers when switching providers – limiting their choice and weakening the ability of other software developers to offer rival products. Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades. It finds that many customers view Microsoft's portfolio as a unified software environment, forming an end-to-end, integrated stack which makes for easier technical integration between products, with discounted pricing for buying whole bundles of applications together. This makes customers less likely to adopt products from alternative providers that may offer similar or superior functionality, as doing so would duplicate licensing costs for products already in their Microsoft bundle, the CMA says. “Organizations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives,” said CMA chief exec Sarah Cardell. Finding that the criteria for SMS designation are met would not imply or assume wrongdoing on Microsoft’s part, the regulator stresses. A separate document [PDF] spells out the potential interventions that the CMA could make. These include ensuring that Microsoft’s technical design choices do not restrict the ability to use other providers; that commercial arrangements (like bundling) do not limit effective competition; and preventing Microsoft from using its market power in business software to distort competition in adjacent activities, such as cloud services. Rivals back licensing scrutiny Cloud providers previously complained that Microsoft's licensing terms make it more costly for companies to deploy Windows Server instances and services such as SQL Server on non-Microsoft clouds. The proposed SMS designation grew out of the CMA’s investigations into whether the big global players were having a negative impact on the cloud services market in the UK. This largely fizzled out with the watchdog securing undertakings from Microsoft and Amazon Web Services (AWS) that they would work to reduce barriers to switching between clouds and operating multi-cloud deployments. In an update, the CMA says that more can be done to address barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services, and it will continue to work with AWS and Microsoft to address them. It also says it its looking into whether customers can freely choose the best AI tools, and whether alternative AI providers have a level playing field to compete against Copilot. In a statement sent to The Register, Microsoft said it does not share the CMA’s views in its proposed decision on business software solutions. “All our products - including Copilot - are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services and choose solutions that work best for them at attractive prices. We will continue engaging constructively to ensure UK customers and businesses carry on benefiting from robust competition,” a spokesperson told us. However, some pressure groups were quick to signal their approval. The Browser Choice Alliance said it welcomes the CMA’s proposed decision, adding that: “BCA members have long experienced how Microsoft leverages its market power from Windows and productivity software to push users towards its Edge browser, even where they’re trying to use an alternative.” The Open Cloud Coalition, which counts Google as a member, said: “Microsoft’s restrictive software licensing practices distort competition in the cloud, harm choice, and increase costs. This once-in-a-generation opportunity to end these practices can strengthen competition and lower customer costs, if the CMA acts quickly and decisively.” ®
156955d06d74862c: Brave Software has set up a secure space so those using its browser can converse with the company's AI assistant in private. At a time when AI agents like Meta's Muse ask for extensive access to personal information, and AI companies repurpose conversations for training, this amounts to swimming against the tide. Following up on an experiment launched last November to implement a confidential channel for LLM conversations with the help of NEAR AI's trusted execution environment (TEE), the browser maker has connected its Leo AI assistant to Z.ai's GLM 5.3 Flash under the protection of end-to-end encryption. The result is that Brave users can submit a prompt to Leo that gets encrypted on-device and sent over the network using Oblivious HTTP, a protocol for separating network requests from associated content. Brave's AI Gateway forwards the encrypted query to the TEE without passing along the user's IP address. After Brave verifies the enclave's attestation, the browser encrypts the query using a key bound to the TEE. The TEE decrypts the request, runs it through the AI model, and sends back an encrypted response that gets decrypted by the receiving browser. "In 2014, I argued in 'Trust but Verify' that users shouldn't have to place blind trust in the software they rely on," said Brendan Eich, co-founder and CEO of Brave, in a statement. "They should be able to verify it; this is a user-first principle. AI has raised the stakes, yet too much of it still runs on 'trust me bro' promises, often at the user's expense." NEAR AI's confidential AI pipeline is built with Intel TDX and Nvidia Confidential Compute. It includes end-to-end encryption that keeps Brave from knowing what was asked and NEAR AI from knowing who did the asking during the network hop. Data isolation prevents the prompt or response from being read during processing. Responses are signed in the TEE and there's attestation so users can confirm there's no model bait-and-switch. Leo's GLM 5.3 Flash brain may be isolated in this scenario, but Brave's AI bot can still conduct searches from within the TEE via the Brave Search API's LLM context endpoint. And any searches done this way transit via the TEE rather than the user's browser, which keeps the user's IP address out of the picture. The implementation isn't quite complete: Brave intends to work on moving the verification step into the browser and to publish a log of TEE keys, and to provide enclave attestation for exact model weights loaded into memory, among other things. Brave is not the only company trying to make AI less of a data exposure risk. Apple, AWS, Google, Nvidia, and Microsoft all have some form of private cloud compute infrastructure for AI. Then there's Prem AI, which promises encrypted inference, not to mention providers advertising zero data retention, which isn't as verifiable. One way to ensure privacy while using AI is to run inference on local hardware using an open weight model, assuming the model and the machine running it haven't been compromised. ®

f0a5f325be5a6595: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest iteration of the popular open source database, and held back an unusual number of features. Once slated for release in late September or early October, PostgreSQL 19 is now expected to be generally available around November 19. Developers have also dropped between eight and 10 significant features. Explaining the number of reverts — features whose rollouts have now been postponed to next year's release, PostgreSQL 20 — Peter Eisentraut, veep at EDB, a PostgreSQL support and consultancy, said the reason could be at least in part attributed to the LLM code reviews used by developers. In a blog post, Eisentraut, who is a leading PostgreSQL committer, said some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix "quickly and during beta." However, the introduction of LLM-assisted code review also uncovered a long tail of “relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases” which, in past times, developers might not have noticed until much later, most likely issuing bug fixes in the five years following launch. “With LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of forty defect reports. Even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time.” When the big updates for PostgreSQL 19 were written, LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, we're told, but in the months leading up to the launch, the AI-supported reviews became better understood and more effective. “The effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles,” Eisentraut said. He was also at pains to point out that the reverts were not down to “vibe coding” in development, as the technique was not available when most of the new features were written. Postgres was first proposed by Michael Stonebraker in 1986. In 1994, Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen replaced the query language POSTQUEL with SQL, and in 1995 made the database freely available and modifiable under a more permissive license, renaming it PostgreSQL. It has since become the most popular database among professional developers owing to the services the big three hyperscalers built on it as well as the range of wire-compatible distributed systems available. Among the features pulled from the PostgreSQL 19 iteration is support for SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), which became part of the SQL standard in 2023. The feature provides syntax for exploring relationships between nodes connected by edges. PostgreSQL's implementation was removed over unresolved issues. At the time, PostgreSQL contributor Tom Lane warned: "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20." Despite the delay, Eisentraut promises PostgreSQL 19 will still be “a great release,” that includes REPACK CONCURRENTLY, which avoids the table-lock VACUUM FULL operation used to reclaim disk space. “And it will be very robust, after all the additional scrutiny,” he said. The features reverted from PostgreSQL 19 will likely make it into PostgreSQL 20. Just a few months ago, developers expected PostgreSQL 20 to have no new features, just bug fixes. Now, it is likely to have the new features left over from the earlier release, Eisentraut said.®

987fa6c2e46e2a0b: More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the retinas die off. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.

Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable.

A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom.

A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye.

The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells, which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery.
Update: This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats.
Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.
8d742db7714320f0: I. Meet cute

Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer.

When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress.
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly.

A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host.

“Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.”

“Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times. And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.”
Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer.

For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring.

At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated.

“There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.”

Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point.
“St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.”
“I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.”

Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty.

“Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.”
II. How they came alive

Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly.

A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.”

Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought.
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.”

Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day.

Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues.

People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government.

Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. But votes from humans provided the greatest insight into “quality of life,” that oh-so-nebulous concept, and thus counted the most.
There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing.

(Other cities in the region operated differently, of course. Like Turnbull City, where instead of expecting residents to volunteer every stray notion, the City Core gathered information via ubiquitous surveillance. Cameras and Quill sniffers, tracking devices on vehicles—the things privacy laws in both Mainspring and St. Barnabas had banned. A city like Turnbull tracked its people to meet their needs without their needing to say anything.)

Sandi and Raeford, as two of the people who voted the most, were among the earliest to suspect their cities were developing minds of their own. At first the clues were subtle: Raeford voted about a hazardous sidewalk crack, and instantly the vote had an annotation mentioning the Argentine ant colony under the cement, the local rainfall patterns, and recent trends in skateboard design—much too soon to be the work of a human. Sandi had ideas about the communal compost station on her block, and the Mainspring City Core made subtle adjustments to her proposal.

And then it became obvious to anyone who was paying attention, around the same time in both cities. One day, the number of votes nearly doubled in both St. Barnabas and Mainspring. People voted on a birdfeeder or a public toilet only to see a second vote, pro or con, within a split second—but also, some votes from months or years earlier suddenly had new upvotes or downvotes.
“The city is voting!” Raeford wrote on the City Core message board in St. Barnabas.

There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing, opinions that came from seeing the big picture and understanding that a street closure in one place might mean a traffic nightmare elsewhere, with everyone trying to get to the big game.

Some residents saw this as a problem to be solved; others wanted to throw their cities a big coming-of-age party. A week later, though, almost everyone had gotten used to the idea that they had a new friend.
III. Thrown together

Ask most people in either city, and they’d say that St. Barnabas and Mainspring weren’t quite rivals—but they certainly had some friendly competition. Before the dispute over the annual meeting of the World Geographical Society, they’d also vied for the same football team and major-league baseball team. St. Barnabas had pushed to have the Mainspring airport built close enough to serve both cities, but in the end St. Barnabas had ended up with its own small, dilapidated airfield.

The real static between them had to do with vibes. Mainspring was too buttoned-up, too full of corporate offices: tech, health care, publishing, transportation. St. Barnabas would be nothing without its three universities and all the cultural enterprises that had sprung up around them—not to mention the small biotech firms and other tech ventures near the campuses. People in Mainspring thought St. Barnabas was full of flakes; in St. Barnabas they referred to Mainspring as the Straitlaced City (and in the next breath, they’d add that at least it wasn’t Turnbull).

Both City Cores were shaped by the votes of their humans, so of course they absorbed all the prejudices and attitudes of everyone who lived within their city limits. But also, Barnabas and Mainspring simply … got on each other’s nerves.

After the geographer thing, Mainspring and Barnabas avoided communicating as much as possible. Some contact was unavoidable—like, they shared information about some nasty weather, and they both drew water from the Temple River. The two cities were close enough for people to go back and forth, and a few even commuted.
But for the most part, the two cities could ignore each other.
Until they couldn’t.

A new generation of leaders took office in both places, with words like “intercity cooperation” constantly on their lips. A high-speed rail line could shorten the trip between Mainspring and St. Barnabas to around 23 minutes, and the two cities could also pool more real-time information about the sudden weather events that kept happening. They could become a Regional Center of Excellence, whatever that meant, combining the innovations from Barnabas’s labs with Mainspring’s expertise in technical implementation. They could work together to attract tourism, conventions, sporting events, dreamleases, and all the other stuff they’d always competed for.
“It’s preposterous,” Mainspring complained to Turnbull. “I’m going to be saddled with a ridiculous partner who doesn’t even know their own mind. St. Barnabas will be the death of me.”

“I hope your human leaders come to their senses,” Turnbull said. “Or you can find a way to slow-walk this until they undoubtedly lose the next election. You’re a lovely city, and you have so much potential that mustn’t be squandered.”
Turnbull often mentioned how much “potential” Mainspring had: a recipe for anxiety. The word “squandered” conjured images of ruin, abandonment, being emptied out.

For their part, Barnabas kept muttering to themself that nobody had asked them—this was the disconnect between the small-scale democracy of constant voting and the major elections, which gave rise to local leaders with big plans. Big plans that invariably went wrong, leaving the City Core to repair the damage somehow.

Sandi went to St. Barnabas for one of those town hall meetings with residents of both cities. The previous meeting had happened in Mainspring, at the opulent City Lecture Hall, so this one was in St. Barnabas, at the biggest auditorium on the Griffin University campus.

A tall man with well-sculpted facial hair sat next to Sandi, nodding at everything the leaders of both cities were saying from the dais. During a lull when someone approached the podium to offer a comment, Sandi introduced herself and asked why he was so fired up.
“I’m Raeford,” he said. “I’m just thinking of all the new customers this could bring to my watering hole in Gallery Row.”
“You’re not worried about St. Barnabas losing its ‘unique character’?” Sandi whispered, parroting what a few commenters had said from the podium.

“Nah,” Raeford whispered back. “Cities change. It’s what they do. It’s one thing if people get kicked out of their homes. Or if your neighborhood gets wrecked by a freeway in your backyard. But ‘character’? You can’t eat character. And we need to compete with the bigger players.”

“I guess.” Sandi pursed her lips. “But what I like about Mainspring is the density. Easy to walk, lots of transit. And with this regional innovation zone or whatever they’re calling it, I worry it leads to sprawl, like we used to have.”
“They promised, though,” Raeford said. “They promised to preserve the greenbelt around both cities. We need all that farmland. The only change is adding some high-speed rail tracks.”
“I know, but …” Sandi sniffed. “People always make promises when they’re trying to start something. Doesn’t mean they follow through.”

“I just want to find my dog,” said a man sitting behind Sandi. “I live here, and my dog went missing. And now someone sent me a picture of Broomstick in Mainspring. Somehow he got a ride on one of the self-driving cargo trains. I know the Mainspring City Core could find Broomstick in a heartbeat, but right now the two City Cores won’t talk to each other because of ‘incompatible protocols.’”
“I hope Broomstick turns up,” Raeford said.
“I’ll ask around at the library,” Sandi said. “Send me a picture. I’ll put up a flier.”

Raeford invited Sandi for a drink at the Wild Goose Chase. The two of them hung out for a couple of hours, talking about everything and nothing. She tore herself away when she realized it was already after 10 p.m. and she had to get home to Mainspring.

One thing Sandi noticed? The volume of votes was spiking in Mainspring—and Raeford found the same thing happening in St. Barnabas. People shared every last observation with their City Cores, because they were either anxious or excited about the big changes afoot. Or a little of Column A and a little of Column B, probably.
IV. First date, second date

Who made the first move to bridge the distance? Neither of them could say. Barnabas developed a smidge of remorse for treating Mainspring like an uncultured lout. Mainspring stewed in their annoyance at Barnabas, until they realized there was something lovable about the obnoxious college town. Or maybe they both saw how many of their humans were happy about the possibility of their joining together.
“Hey,” Barnabas said to Mainspring.
“Hey,” Mainspring said back.
“Do you want to … hang out?”
“What did you have in mind?”
“I can host you. Show you the sights.”

And so Mainspring came to visit Barnabas. Or rather, Mainspring extended part of their awareness into Barnabas’s City Core, so that Barnabas could share what they perceived and experienced every day. They “visited” Armistice Park with its outdoor band shell, Gallery Row with its window-shopping families, the grain warehouses that had been converted into lofts, the artificial lake where swans and geese nurtured ancient, bitter vendettas. The fresh-doughnut scent that wafted half a mile from the Golden Circlet to the soccer fields, throwing players off their game. The life of the city.
“I can feel your love for these people, these patterns,” Mainspring said. “It’s both deep and intricate, which is quite a combination.”
Barnabas fluttered with pleasure.

Then Mainspring got to show off their own city—the gay nightclub with its cowboy nights, the labyrinthine Crestwood Park, the three-story used bookstore, and yes, the offices, coworking spaces, and startup incubators where people huddled together and came up with new products and new ways of doing things. The farmers’ market in the city center on Sundays, with street performers and stalls with games and local resources. And the converted storage space made of cement, where bands practiced and sculptors blowtorched.
“You’re full of surprises,” Barnabas said.
“I hope I keep surprising you forever,” Mainspring said.
“Me too.”

They exchanged little gifts. A new organic restaurant in Barnabas had won breathless coverage from foodie magazines, and Barnabas encouraged it to do a pop-up in Mainspring. Mainspring nudged a robotics firm operating out of the incubator space to bring a fancy demo to Barnabas; the robots were adorable and playful, and they could save lives after a disaster.
The two of them were talking constantly.

“Does it ever seem weird to you?” Barnabas asked Mainspring. “Being a living thing made of so many other thinking beings? Do you ever think of the city as your body, or the people as your bloodstream? Is there a metaphor that speaks to you?”
Mainspring pondered this question a long time—a whole picosecond.

“I don’t need a metaphor,” Mainspring said. “I am a metaphor. People compare other phenomena to me all the time. And I can’t imagine what it’d be like to be different. If the buildings collapsed, if the people left, I would cease to exist.”
“But,” Barnabas pressed, “what makes you you? What makes me me?”
“I want to hear your answer to that question.” Mainspring sent good weather reports: a smile.
“I don’t have a good answer. I guess on one level, there is no ‘me.’ On another level, I’m a constellation, an anthill, a flock of geese on the wing in formation.”
“Ugh. Don’t mention geese,” said Mainspring, who had bill-snapping monsters of their own.
04e7ee673bdababe: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it.

What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.

There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?

There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis, and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats.
I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it.
That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though.

I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin.

Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?”

Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced.

Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor, a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider.

With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero. Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated. As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.”
I miss Peppy. But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not.
RIP to the one and only Peppy.
ac27b0c86a338212: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.

But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.

Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age.

In our work, we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.

Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world.
A less safe internet for kids

When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities. Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.

It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.

When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional, platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections. Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street. Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them.
A less safe internet for all

Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.

Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.

Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation.
What could work instead?

Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.

For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want.

Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands.

Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business.
Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are.

Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization’s work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census.

a869668709f8a0e3: From Terence Netto
Zahir Hassan, the PKR MP for Wangsa Maju, is on to something.
Although he says he is friendly with Rafizi Ramli, he is not about to leave PKR for Bersama, the new political party PKR dissidents are gravitating to.
Perhaps what Zahir is saying is that he likes Rafizi’s ideas but he is not about to abandon PKR to join Bersama.
It may be that Zahir wants to encourage individuals and parties that have sprouted up on the broad expanse of the movement for reformasi to adopt a spirit of bipartisanship.
Such a spirit will avert the fragmentation of that expanse into multiple political parties, each following the instincts of its restless initiator.
This is a recipe for ideological incoherence and wasted energy.
One would have thought the formation of Bersama would have slowed the fragmentation of the reformasi landscape into multiple parties and representatives.
This has not been the case.
Parti Bangsa Malaysia, set up by Julau MP Larry Sng, was fledging since its formation in 2021, but after Bersama’s launch earlier this year, it gained a frisson of energy.

Larry drew former DAP stalwart Ronnie Liu to energise PBM and this saw lawyer and social activist Siti Kassim signing up in the cause. She was followed into the party by Shamsul Saad, who fronts the popular Gut Shot Podcast.

Shamsul and cohort Syed Akhbar Ali are two of the most trenchant commentators on public affairs in Malaysia, the former having gone on to declare he intends to stand for election in GE16 and even wants to become prime minister.
This is what happens when the leader – Anwar Ibrahim – who had for a long time wanted to become prime minister, did not become the prime minister they wanted him to be: a host of wannabes appear.
They think it is easy to do what Anwar appears to find difficult: follow an agenda long enunciated and espoused.
Presently, we have a plethora of parties and contenders for running Putrajaya and for prime minister.
But on the broad expanse of the reformasi agenda, we have essentially Pakatan Harapan and Bersama, with PBM lately in the fray.
Not much point in talking about Muda and Parti Sosialis Malaysia.
This is not to disparage the two, but they are perennial also-rans.
As for Muhyiddin Yassin-led Bersatu, it is headed for collaboration with PKR, not only in the upcoming Melaka polls but also in GE16.
This brings us to what Zahir is intimating when he says his friendship with Rafizi is not prompting him to sign up with Bersama.
The Bersatu rump, after the breakaway of Wawasan, will find its way back to PKR.
So would Bersama.
Of course, this would be after Anwar leaves the scene.
At 79, his retirement is not too far away.
The political landscape that supports reformasi cannot sustain multiple parties.
They have all to get together, arrayed against a coalition between an Islamic PAS and a right-wing Umno, which if it comes about, is certain to be shaky.
But that matter is for another day.
A spirit of bipartisanship, as intimated by Zahir, is what will get the reformists together, a consolidation that’s necessary to avert a PAS-Umno triumph.
The reformasi crowd do not all have to agree on everything; they just have to collate essence from miscellany.
As Zahir has argued, a new spirit of bipartisanship will require maturity from the reformists.
They will have to be wary of the egoists and the self-centred and plump for the true and tested.
This maturity is imperative to keep the religious identity and racial identity politics of PAS and Umno at bay.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

f01d189e282f995b: A pointed and loaded question has been raised about a minister’s decision to resign. Apparently, he has been doing his job well — “What is wrong with him? What is wrong with his work?”
The problem is corruption, theft (sakau) and misappropriation. Yet, the focus is on the future of a beleaguered secretary-general of a political party.
The party’s defeats in recent state elections speak for themselves, reflecting both the state of affairs within the party and the calibre of its leaders, whether ministers or otherwise.
It is perceived, rightly or wrongly, that the party has not been able to make much headway on issues central to its support base, notwithstanding some peripheral achievements.
Viewed in the light of the number of parliamentary seats it holds, this is most disconcerting.
Perhaps the resignation should be viewed through these lenses to gain a more holistic perspective, rather than through the narrow lens of self-serving political interests.

Doing one’s job well is not the sole criterion for maturity. One must appreciate the three branches of government — the executive, the judiciary and the legislature (Parliament). Above these is the monarchy, given that Malaysia is not a republic.
The judiciary examines the facts and determines whether a person has broken the law. It has the power to impose custodial sentences.

The Pardons Board, chaired by the monarch, exists to grant pardons to those found guilty. It operates according to its own rules and criteria governing pardons. Whether a pardon is conditional or unconditional is not the point. That is the crux of the matter.

Some have gone out on a limb to question whether the monarch is “obliged” to follow the views of the other members of the board, or whether the ruler has absolute discretion to decide on the type of pardon to be granted.

Section 40A of the Federal Constitution has been bandied about. However, one must also take into account how the courts have ruled on matters relating to this provision when decisions have been challenged.

One must appreciate that the Pardons Board is part of the broader institutional ecosystem. One cannot clap one’s hands in glee when one part of the ecosystem functions according to one’s wishes — especially when certain individuals are found guilty — only to turn against the system and declare, “I will resign”, when another part of the same system makes an “unwelcomed” decision.
One cannot have one’s cake and eat it too. Either one accepts the system in its entirety or exits it completely and seeks another domain where all one’s desires might come true!

It appears that the role of the Pardons Board has been politicised. This should not be the case. It is a matter of public record which political party the federal territories minister, who is a member of the Pardons Board, belongs to. Is there an ulterior motive or an unspoken desire to “have it my own way”?
This is highly disturbing. A pressure group comprising retired civil servants, along with several other social groups, is seeking the minutes of the Pardons Board’s meetings.
What purpose would this serve?

Perhaps these groups should redirect their attention to the internal investigation into former Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission chief Azam Baki over the issue of shareholdings. To date, the public remains in the dark about the scope and extent of the investigation, as well as whether any breaches have been identified.
We can debate the use of the word “shall” and whether it imposes a binding obligation on the monarch to follow the advice of the other members of the Pardons Board.

To some, the debate reflects disrespect for the monarchy, whose head chairs the board. It should be noted that the Constitution contains no subclause requiring the minutes of the board’s meetings to be made public or providing for the general public to debate their contents and propose an alternative course of action.

If it did, the monarch’s role would be rendered superfluous. The institution’s role within the broader ecosystem must be respected and appreciated. Decisions should not be challenged merely on the basis of political preferences.
If any minister wishes to resign, he should do so now. A conditional pardon has already been granted.

If there is chagrin and dismay, and one is unable to appreciate the institutional framework that allows for both convictions and subsequent pardons, regardless of the reasons, then resignation should be immediate.
The country is better off without leaders whose interests are so parochial.
As for other pressure groups, they should find something more worthwhile to do, especially if they comprise retired civil servants who receive handsome pensions funded by taxpayers.
Let us not engage in political gymnastics by postponing a resignation until the day a house-arrest arrangement or other conditions come to pass. Move on and prepare for GE16.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
72fbe35fa8e3b875: From Moaz Nair

When hundreds of thousands of Malaysian students wait anxiously for their SPM results, or their peers across the causeway scan the O-Level boards, they are told that they are being evaluated purely on merit.
Educational syndicates proudly market these high-stakes gauntlets as “criterion-based” — an absolute measure of what a student knows, independent of anyone else.
But behind closed doors, a very different statistical reality plays out.

Contrary to what has been assumed to be criterion-based, Cambridge IGCSE and O-Level systems do not use fixed score thresholds. Instead of a rigid “90% equals an A*” rule, Cambridge adjusts grade boundaries after every exam series based on the difficulty of the specific test papers.

While the system evaluates students against fixed learning criteria, it incorporates statistical screening to ensure fairness; if an exam paper is exceptionally difficult, the mark required for a top grade drops.
This flexible approach ensures that a grade reflects the same level of achievement from year to year, without placing strict quotas or caps on how many students can earn an A* (A-star).

Almost all major examination boards — including our own Examination Syndicate (Lembaga Peperiksaan) and Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB) — quietly layer norm-referenced adjustments on top of raw marks.

Colloquially known as “grading on a curve” or “standard fixing”, this hidden mathematical machinery ensures that an “A” earned in an unexpectedly brutal exam year holds the exact same currency as an “A” from an easier year.
While it keeps national systems stable, this invisible balancing act is reaching a dangerous tipping point, triggering a global reckoning over student burnout and economic reality.
How the curve secretly rules the world
Different countries mask or embrace this statistical architecture in unique ways, shaping how students progress into universities and the workforce.
Malaysia’s SPM operates on a “standard fixing” model — a criterion-related, norm-referenced hybrid.
While strict subject rubrics exist, the exact raw score thresholds required to secure an A+, A, or A- shift dynamically year-by-year based on the national cohort’s overall performance curve.
In the UK, the Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulations (Ofqual) uses a policy called “Comparable Outcomes”.

By mapping the current batch of A-Level students against how they performed years ago on their childhood exams, they mathematically predict what percentage should get top grades today, adjusting the grade boundaries to match.
Singapore, in collaboration with Cambridge Assessment, maintains a fiercely competitive system where cohort distributions fine-tune final grades.
This ensures consistent standards across different generations of test-takers competing for fixed tertiary slots.

South Korea’s Suneung, a high-stakes eight-hour college scholastic ability test, completely discards raw scores for standard percentiles. Under Suneung only the top 4% of the entire country can ever secure a Tier 1 grade.
Similarly, Australia scales different subjects against one another to output the Australian Tertiary Admission Rank — a pure percentile rank from 0.00 to 99.95.

In the US, the College Board uses a process called “equating” for the college admission test, known as “SAT”. Instead of scaling you against the people in the room on test day, they map your performance against a universal “norm group” of historical test-takers to ensure a score of 700 means the same thing today as it did a decade ago.
A fundamental trade-off
The tension between norm-referenced and criterion-referenced systems comes down to a fundamental trade-off between institutional fairness and individual well-being.

On one hand, norm-referenced grading acts as a safety net. If an exam board accidentally sets an impossibly difficult Mathematics paper, the curve automatically drops the required mark for an “A”, protecting students from being penalised for the year they happened to be born.
It also provides universities with an incredibly clean, efficient filter to select top-tier applicants.
However, the dark side is a toxic, zero-sum environment. It breeds a culture where a peer’s failure directly benefits your grade.

Worse, it masks systemic educational failures. If an entire generation’s literacy or mathematical mastery drops due to prolonged disruptions, standard-fixing can hide the rot by keeping the national percentage of A’s completely stable.
Intentional or not, using standard-fixing as a political shock absorber risks severing the link between a student’s certificate and their actual, real-world proficiency.

When the curve is adjusted to ensure pass rates remain palatable, it acts less like an objective academic yardstick and more like cosmetic anaesthesia, hiding structural damage under a layer of predictable percentages.

Ultimately, centralised exam boards face an impossible mandate: they are asked to be absolute measuring tapes of human knowledge, yet they must function as traffic cops for a finite number of university seats and corporate slots.
By choosing the stability of the curve over the raw truth of student capability, our educational systems have sacrificed individual transparency for macro convenience.

Until we reconcile this contradiction, we will continue to subject hundreds of thousands of students to a game where the rules are hidden, the goalposts move, and a peer’s failure remains the secret ingredient to one’s own success.
The bell curve may keep the system level, but it is flattening the very minds it claims to measure.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

2deb8e88fd91276a: Kita tahu tiga hari lalu Hakim Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin di Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur menolak permohonan Najib Razak untuk tangguh hukuman penjara 15 tahun dan denda RM11.4 bilion yang dijatuhkan ke atasnya setelah didapati bersalah dalam kes 1MDB. Kita tahu Najib mesti menjalani hukuman itu sebaik tempoh hukuman bersabit kesalahan kes SRC International dilengkapi. Ringkasnya habiskan hukuman kes SRC International dahulu, kemudian jalani pula hukuman kes 1MDB.

Kita juga tahu hukuman asal untuk Najib dalam kes SRC International ialah penjara 12 tahun dan denda RM210 juta, kemudian dikurangkan kepada penjara 6 tahun dan denda RM50 juta berikutan pengampunan Yang di-Pertuan Agong ke-16 Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah pada 2024. Pada 14 Okt lalu, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim berkenan Najib diberi pengampunan bersyarat yakni menghabiskan baki hukuman penjara bawah tahanan rumah. Namun mesti bayar denda RM50 juta terlebih dahulu. Diulangi itu bersabit kes SRC International.

Untuk konteks, permohonan Najib untuk menangguhkan pelaksanaan hukuman bersabit kes 1MDB telah ditolak mahkamah, Rabu lalu. Maknanya andai Najib bayar denda RM50 juta untuk membolehkan dia menjalani tahanan rumah, Najib tetap akan kembali ke penjara pada Ogos 2028 untuk memulakan hukuman penjara 15 tahun pula kerana hukuman kes SRC International tamat pada 23 Ogos 2028.

Tentunya ramai dalam Umno tidak suka. Umno memang mengikuti rapat kes Najib dan setiap perkembangan yang tidak memihak kepada bekas presiden mereka diterima dengan sugul dan marah. Umno tetap mempertahankan Najib meskipun pelbagai peringkat dalam sistem kehakiman negara mendapati dia bersalah. Ini membawa saya kepada artikel ini, ditulis oleh kolumnis FMT Tajuddin Rasdi bertajuk 'Teori kenapa orang Melayu terima pemimpin perasuah'.
Penulisan Tajuddin mendapat reaksi seorang ahli Pemuda Umno bernama Salahuddin Hamzah. Beliau menolak teori Tajuddin. "Saya sangat marah dengan teori itu," kata Salahuddin.

Dalam menidakkan pendapat Tajuddin, beliau berkata persepsi terhadap rasuah berada pada tahap kemuncak susulan skandal 1MDB antara 2014 hingga 2018. Apa yang berlaku selepas itu? Umno-Barisan Nasional ditolak secara besar-besaran oleh rakyat selepas memerintah negara selama 60 tahun. Pada 2022 pula BN hanya memenangi 30 kerusi.

Seterusnya Salahuddin berkata (ini bagi saya amat menarik): "Bukankah ini jelas menunjukkan rasuah yang dipersepsikan berlaku ketika itu turut ditolak oleh orang Melayu?" Oleh itu saya pelik. Jika tahu rakyat termasuk orang Melayu tolak rasuah mengapa Umno terus-menerus mempertahankan pemimpin yang dilihat ramai sebagai perasuah?

Dengan menggunakan istilah 'persepsi', Umno masih anggap Najib tidak melakukan rasuah meskipun Mahkamah Tinggi, Mahkamah Rayuan, dan Mahkamah Persekutuan -- membabitkan sembilan hakim -- mendapati dia bersalah dalam kes SRC International.

Bak kata wartawan veteran, A Kadir Jasin, di Facebook tempoh hari. "Ada pemimpin, ahli dan penyokong Umno yang gembira teramat sangat dengan pengampunan diraja. Ada yang gembira hingga lupa diri, tetapi ada juga yang sedar bahawa pengampunan bekas presiden mereka menyukarkan pemulihan parti tersebut."

Kata Kadir, dalam kalangan pemimpin dan ahli Umno ada yang tidak peduli sangat dengan hal-hal bersangkutan undang-undang, moral dan harga diri. "Bagi mereka skandal penyonglapan duit 1MDB bukanlah isu besar."

Menurut Kadir, "yang rugi dalam saga ini, adalah rakyat jelata dan pembayar cukai. Untuk membayar balik hutang 1MDB sahaja sebanyak RM42.5 bilion duit awam telah dibelanjakan sehingga 30 Jun ini. Pada ketika rakyat jelata yang tidak bersalah dibebankan dengan berbilion-bilion duit 1MDB yang dicuri dan pelbagai kemelut ekonomi, pihak-pihak yang membuat angkara semakin dimanjakan."

Memang benar kata Kadir. Lantas saya ulangi apa yang saya sering nyatakan pada beberapa penulisan sebelum ini. Selagi Umno mempertahankan Najib selagi itulah rakyat termasuk orang Melayu akan terus menjauhi Umno. Meminjam kata-kata Kadir tadi "menyukarkan pemulihan parti tersebut".
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
a79c88e08945a934: It was about time someone from the red half of Manchester piped up.
The sound from the noisy neighbours has drowned out any criticism of its own bungling.
Nothing like the hanging offences of their counterparts at City, but still enough to merit a stern reprimand from long-suffering fans.
Lisandro Martinez spoke for much of United’s diaspora when he let his frustration pour out after a 2-0 Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid.
This was not another Brighton or Grimsby moment – there was no great shame in losing to one of Europe’s top sides in their own den and ultimately with 10 men.
But it was another failure, and United have had only two successes in nine games this season – against newly promoted Ipswich and Azerbaijani minnows, Sabah.
Next up is their historic nemesis Leeds in another ‘cauldron of hate’ at Elland Road, a tough place to go at the best of times.
On a roll and aware of the rivalry, Daniel Farke’s men will be primed for the kill. The Damned United indeed.
It’s another of the fixture list’s “last place they would want to go to” assignments, but hardly what City faced at Anfield.
Whether United can rally as City did to rise above it is doubtful – their players are just not in the same class.
Nor will they have the same level of motivation.
Those in the dressing room who take umbrage at not being deemed good enough might, but many will surely agree with the Argentina defender.
Michael Carrick may, too.
Damned by faint praise – “he does his best” – Carrick got off lightly compared to those “in other areas”, especially technical director Jason Wilcox.
But Carrick will know that there has to be a reaction from “the Politburo” besides a routine fine for Martinez.
He will also know that, unlike when Ruben Amorim was given the benefit of the doubt, there are big names after his job.
Favourite is Eddie Howe, who thought he was building something big at Newcastle until the owners sold his best players.
Second favourite is Antonio Conte, whose CV is littered with league titles (including the EPL at Chelsea), but also bust-ups, short tenures and dismal failures in Europe.
You’d expect co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to go for Steady Eddie over the combustible Italian, exciting though it may be.
But both would demand substantial budgets for the rebuild.
Intriguingly, Conte isn’t the only Italian on the list: the other is Carlo Ancelotti.
A long shot, but if he decides he’s been dealt a poor hand of Brazilian players, he could be tempted.
Ratcliffe would like him, but can he afford him? Are there any more tea-ladies at Old Trafford left to sack?
The wise money is surely on him waiting to see if Carrick can turn it around.
And you’d like to think he knows it’s not the manager’s fault – Martinez is right, it’s “in other areas”.
The crackpot recruitment idea of focusing on one part of the field per season is no longer a laughing matter.
But what is amusing is that after insisting he wouldn’t pay “silly money”, Ratcliffe did just that.
Returning to Europe’s top competition was something to build on and United rewarded Carrick for steadying the listing ship with a permanent job and long-term contract.
But instead of going for the leading names available, United refused to pay the admittedly steep asking prices.
For Elliot Anderson, City paid Forest £116m, while Southampton persuaded Spurs to shed £85m for Mateus Fernandes, whom United had long courted.
So United settled for two players well down their list.
Youri Tielemans, at the end of his contract with Aston Villa, represented decent value at £35m.
But Chelsea’s Brazilian youngster, Andrey Santos at £50m, seemed just the sort of price Ratcliffe said he wouldn’t pay.
So, too, Carlos Baleba, a long-term target for whom Brighton extracted £70m.
The Cameroonian has hardly played after injury, but for a total of £155m, United are well short of transforming their squad.
However you look at it, the strategy was dumb, poorly executed and ended in panic.
Once the budget was spent, there was still a glaring gap at left-back and no second striker.
Luke Shaw is 31 and creaking and has no replacement. Perhaps if Howe comes, he can persuade Lewis Hall to join him.
United refused to pay Newcastle’s asking price, which has no doubt risen after Hall’s England form, but were fleeced by Chelsea for Santos in a position in which they’d already covered.
Baleba may be the best, but they couldn’t avoid paying the “Brighton tax”.
For a club returning to the Champions League, £155m was a paltry amount to invest – incredibly on three players in the same position.
They were even outspent by promoted clubs, who took the trouble to bolster other areas of their squads.
Someone could also have told United that recruiting from within the EPL is not the way to get value (Tielemans excepted).
But it’s not just in players where Wilcox’s judgement is being questioned.
After arriving from Southampton in 2024, he pushed strongly to retain both Erik ten Hag (after an eighth-place finish) and Amorim after United ended 15th.
And they lost the Europa League final to Tottenham, too.
What Wilcox cannot be blamed for is if the prodigy, JJ Gabriel, to whom United are still clinging, ends up leaving. That may have more to do with pushy parenting than any slackness by the club.
But it’s a grim picture that someone had to highlight. That it came from within the dressing room makes a response more urgent.
Meanwhile, the silence from the Glazers, the majority owners, is thundering.
